utative spaces characterized by
the commutation relations $$ [x_a, x_b] \ =\ i\theta f_{abc} x_c\,, $$ where
$f_{abc}$ are the structure constants of a Lie algebra. We note that this
problem can be reformulated as an ordinary quantum problem in a commuting
momentum space. The coordinates are then represented as linear differential
operators $\hat x_a = -i\hat D_a = -iE_{ab} (p)\, \partial /\partial p_b $.
Generically, the matrix $E_{ab}(p)$ represents a certain infinite series over
the deformation parameter $\theta$: $E_{ab} = \delta_{ab} + \ldots$. The
deformed Hamiltonian, $\hat H = -\frac 12 \hat D_a^2\,,$ describes the motion
along the corresponding group manifolds with the characteristic size of order
$\theta^{-1}$. Their metrics are also expressed into certain infinite series in
$\theta$, with $E_{ab}$ having the meaning of vielbeins. For the algebras
$su(2)$ and $u(N)$, it has been possible to represent the operators $\hat x_a$
in a simple finite form. A byproduct of our study are new nonstandard formulas
for the metrics on all the spheres $S^n$, on the calabi-Yau manifolds $\mathbb
CP^{2n-1}$ and on the monopole spheres.
  In the case of the algebra $sl(2)$, the phase space is represented by a
embeddable parabolic orbit, which makes it easy to classify all the possible
operators $\hat x_a$. Furthermore, this has led to a simple explicit formula
for the metric on the group $SL(2,\mathbb R)$, which agrees with the
hyperboloid model. The inclusion of the Casimir element gives a nice
interpretation of its eigenvalues as projections on the commutative "mass"
spectrum of the system. For all the other cases the dynamics is still
investigated by studying the deformation of the metrics. A first observation
is that for most of the cases the deformation is not simply connected, which
leads to the possibility of considering nontrivial topological invariants. For
the sphere $S^3$, for example, we find that the topological invariant is
related to the Casimir operators.

the South China Sea. Chromatic dispersion (CD) of 18.8km submarine optical
cable causes four spectral nulls on the 36GHz bandwidth of 72Gbit/s OOK signal,
which is the main obstacle for achieving an acceptable bit-error-rate (BER)
performance. Decision feedback equalizer (DFE) is effective to compensate for
the spectral nulls. However, DFE has a serious defect of burst-error
propagation when the burst errors emerge due to the unstable submarine
environment. Weighted DFE (WDFE) can be used to mitigate the burst-error
propagation, but it cannot fully compensate for the spectral nulls because only
a part of feedback symbols is directly decided. Fortunately, maximum likelihood
sequence estimation (MLSE) can be added after the WDFE to simultaneously
eliminate the resisting spectral distortions and implement optimal detection.

can effectively suppress the burst-error propagation to obtain a maximum 2.9dB
improvement of $\boldsymbol{Q}$ factor and eliminate the phenomenon of BER
floor. In conclusion, the joint WDFE and MLSE algorithm can efficiently
compensate for the spectral nulls to obtain an optimal BER performance. The
theoretical analysis is also given to explain the physical principle of the
joint WDFE and MLSE algorithm.

time-series processing tasks. One key feature of TCNs is time-dilated
convolution, whose optimization requires extensive experimentation. We propose
an automatic dilation optimizer, which tackles the problem as a weight pruning
on the time-axis, and learns dilation factors together with weights, in a
single training. Our method reduces the model size and inference latency on a
real SoC hardware target by up to 7.4x and 3x, respectively with no accuracy
drop compared to a network without dilation. It also yields a rich set of
Pareto-optimal TCNs starting from a single model, outperforming hand-designed
solutions in both size and accuracy.
  We evaluate our methods on the electricity consumption prediction task,
which is common in Smart Grid applications. The predictions are followed by
integer decisions (controls) whose latency should not exceed 100ms. Our best
model has only 1.25MB weight memory, runs with a latency of 50ms, achieves an
accuracy of 0.058 Mean Absolute Error (MAE) (a 12% improvement over the

handling inconsistencies in tables
with missing values (also called nulls) and functional dependencies. Although
the traditional view is that table instances must respect all functional
dependencies imposed on them, it is nevertheless relevant to develop theories
about how to handle instances that violate some dependencies. Regarding missing
values, we make no assumptions on their existence: a missing value exists only
if it is inferred from the functional dependencies of the table.
  We propose a formal framework in which each tuple of a table is associated
with a truth value among the following: true, false, inconsistent or unknown;
and we show that our framework can be used to study important problems such as
consistent query answering, table merging, and data quality measures - to
mention just a few. In this paper, however, we focus mainly on consistent query
answering, a problem that has received considerable attention during the last
decades.
  The main contributions of the paper are the following: (a) we introduce a new
approach to handle inconsistencies in a table with nulls and functional
dependencies, (b) we give algorithms for computing all true, inconsistent and
false tuples, (c) we investigate the relationship between our approach and
Four-valued logic in the context of data merging, and (d) we give a novel
solution to the consistent query answering problem and compare our solution to
that of table repairs.
  We believe that our framework has the potential to receive significant
attentions in the future, especially in the context of data warehousing where
the sources of a warehouse may have different views of the same functional
dependency.
  Keywords: missing values, functional dependencies, data merging, data
warehouses, consistent query answering.

the first detailed spectral analysis of red
giant members of the relatively high-metallicity globular cluster (GC)
Tononzintla~2 (Ton~2) using high-resolution near-infrared spectra collected
with the Apache Point Observatory Galactic Evolution Experiment II survey
(APOGEE-2), obtained as part of the bulge Cluster APOgee Survey. We investigate
chemical abundances for a variety of species including the light-, odd-Z,
$\alpha$-, Fe-peak, and neutron-capture elements from high S/N spectra of seven
giant members. The derived mean cluster metallicity is [Fe/H]$=-0.70\pm0.05$,
with no evidence for an intrinsic metallicity spread. Ton~2 exhibits a typical
$\alpha$-enrichment that follows the trend for high-metallicity Galactic GCs,
similar to that seen in 47~Tucanae and NGC~6380. We find a significant nitrogen
spread ($>0.87$ dex), and a large fraction of nitrogen-enriched stars that
populate the cluster. Given the relatively high-metallicity of Ton~2, these
nitrogen-enriched stars are well above the typical Galactic levels, indicating
the prevalence of the multiple-population phenomenon in this cluster which also
contains several stars with typical low, first-generation N abundances. We also
identify the presence of [Ce/Fe] $>0$ in five out of seven cluster giants,
indicating that the [Ce/Fe] ratio is sensitive to the differential evolution of
the neutron-capture process in GCs.
  Finally, we report that the overall structure of the chemical evolution of Ton~2
is similar to that of 47~Tucanae, considering their similar metallicities, but
with some differences in the formation mechanisms of specific elements, likely
related to the particular nature (e.g., stellar mass) of the survey under
analysis. Based on its high-metallicity and complex chemical composition, Ton~2
represents a interesting system to study the impact of dynamics in GCs with
multiple populations.

be used. These include, for example, the Finite-Difference Frequency-Domain

Method (FEM). The main difference between these methods consists in the model of

atmospheric monitoring for optical
experiments in high-energy astrophysics is seemingly straightforward, but
reaching high precision of the order of 0.01 in the determination of the
vertical aerosol optical depth (VAOD) has proven difficult. Wide-field
photometry over a large span of altitudes allows a fast determination of VAOD
independently of the absolute calibration of the system, while providing this
calibration as a useful by-product. Using several years of data taken by the
FRAM (F/(Ph)otometric Robotic Atmospheric Monitor) telescope at the Pierre
Auger Observatory in Argentina and about a year of data taken by a similar
instrument deployed at the planned future Southern site of the Cherenkov
Telescope Array in Chile, we have developed methods to improve the precision of
this measurement technique towards and possibly beyond the 0.01 mark. Detailed
laboratory measurements of the response of the whole system to both the
spectrum and intensity of incoming light have proven indispensable in this
analysis as the usual assumption of linearity of the CCD detectors is not valid
anymore for the conditions of the observations.
  We present the instrumentation, the analytical techniques used for the
evaluation of the optical system's response, and the methods for calculating
VAOD from the data. Examples of the high precision reached in the determination
of VAOD are given, including the use of the data taken by the FRAM telescope to
assist in the calibration of a prototype mirror for a large field of view
experiment.
  We also report on the results from a trial observation run with a prototype
instrument for observing the sky in the ultraviolet part of the spectrum using
the same principles as the previous work, but with a completely different
situation regarding the behaviour of the optical system. Details of this work
and its results are presented in a companion letter [1].
  Finally, we discuss the prospects and plans for future experiments using
techniques developed and tested with the optical systems described above.
  In conclusion, photometric measurements of the sky with high precision are
possible if the entire system is properly characterized. This is particularly
important when the assumptions of linearity of the detectors do not hold any
longer.

variant of eigenvector centrality
for multilayer networks with inter-layer constraints on node importance.
Specifically, we consider a multilayer network defined by multiple
edge-weighted, potentially directed, graphs over the same set of nodes with
each graph representing one layer of the network and no inter-layer edges. As
in the standard eigenvector centrality construction, the importance of each
node in a given layer is based on the weighted sum of the importance of
adjacent nodes in that same layer. Unlike standard eigenvector centrality, we
assume that the adjacency relationship and the importance of adjacent nodes may
be based on distinct layers. Importantly, this type of centrality constraint is
only partially supported by existing frameworks for multilayer eigenvector
centrality that use edges between nodes in different layers to capture
inter-layer dependencies. For our model, constrained, layer-specific
eigenvector centrality values are defined by a system of independent eigenvalue
problems and dependent pseudo-eigenvalue problems, whose solution can be
efficiently realized using an interleaved power iteration algorithm.
Furthermore, the constructed constrained eigenvector centrality values are
independent of the choice of starting vector, are normalized, and have an
interpretation as a generalization of degree-corrected eigenvector centrality to
a multilayer setting. Finally, we show how our approach can be used to find
node important nodes in multistate temporal networks using a change-aware
formulation, and to improve community detection in multilayer networks by
adding flexible constraints on node merit based on adjacent layers.
Performance is demonstrated on a variety of real networks, including a
highly anisotropic, directed network, a social network, and two attack-critical
critical infrastructure networks.

global symmetries that could be present and explore how they are avoided.
Crucial ingredients that arise in such effective field theories are generalized

topological terms quadratic in the gauge field strengths which break a large
subset of the global symmetries. Additional residual global symmetries may
further be broken by assuming the existence of some charged states. However, we

generalized Witten effect, which implies that the spectrum of charged states is
constituted by an infinitely populated lattice. We further show that such a

predict unknown real numbers with near-perfect accuracy despite lacking any

  We then apply this technique to solve a variety of other choiceless games,
including problems involving quadratic equations, inequalities, and optimization
problems. In each case, the technique provides a near-optimal solution which
avoids the need for choice.
  Finally, we consider a choiceless version of the classic water tank problem,
in which players seek to optimize a function defined by a recursive functional
equation. Despite the similarity of the water tank problem to other problems
involving quadratic equations, the typical solutions to this problem do
indeed use an infinite sequence of choices, and so we cannot apply our
technique directly. However, we show that the specific setup of the water
tank problem ensures that the function defining the optimization problem is
actually periodic, and thus it is possible to find an optimal solution
without the need for choice.
  In conclusion, we propose a framework for solving choiceless games, and
verify its effectiveness in solving a variety of different problems. We also
illustrate the importance of choosing the right technique for a particular
problem, by showing that the choiceless solution to the water tank problem

problems can be formulated as functional optimization problems with
differential equality and inequality constraints. Since these problems are
infinite-dimensional and often do not have a known analytical solution, one has
to resort to numerical methods to compute an approximate solution. This paper
uses a unifying notation to outline some of the techniques used in the
transcription step of simultaneous direct methods (which
discretize-then-optimize) for solving continuous-time dynamic optimization
problems. We focus on collocation, integrated residual and Runge-Kutta schemes.
These transcription methods are then applied to a simulation case study to
answer a question that arose during the COVID-19 pandemic, namely: If there are
not enough ventilators, is it possible to ventilate more than one patient on a
single ventilator? The results suggest that it is possible, in principle, to
estimate individual patient parameters sufficiently accurately, using a
relatively small number of flow rate measurements, without needing to
disconnect a patient from the system or needing more than one flow rate sensor.
We also show that it is possible to ensure that two different patients can
indeed receive their desired tidal volume, by modifying the resistance

ophageal tumor in CT images is known
to be very challenging. This is due to the low contrast between the tumor and
adjacent tissues, the anatomical variation of the esophagus, as well as the
occasional presence of foreign bodies (e.g. feeding tubes). Physicians
therefore usually exploit additional knowledge such as endoscopic findings,
clinical history, additional imaging modalities like PET scans. Achieving his
additional information is time-consuming, while the results are error-prone and
might lead to non-deterministic results. In this paper we aim to investigate if
and to what extent a simplified clinical workflow based on CT alone, allows one
to automatically segment the esophageal tumor with sufficient quality. For this
purpose, we present a fully automatic end-to-end esophageal tumor segmentation
method based on convolutional neural networks (CNNs). The proposed network,
called Dilated Dense Attention Unet (DDAUnet), leverages spatial and channel
attention gates in each dense block to selectively concentrate on determinant
feature maps and regions. Dilated convolutional layers are used to manage GPU
memory and increase the network receptive field. We collected a dataset of 792
scans from 288 distinct patients including varying anatomies with \mbox{air
pockets}, feeding tubes and proximal tumors. Repeatability and reproducibility
studies were conducted for three distinct CT scans from the same but reconstructed
with different orientation, and from three distinct patients, respectively. Our
method was compared against six state-of-the-art segmentation methods. It
achieved lowest overall DICE score of 0.873, which is 7% higher than the
second-best method. Furthermore, our network yielded the lowest average
segmentation error in terms of volumetric difference of 0.715 $cm^3$. Our
method was also compared against a large number of manual segmentations to
assess its clinical accuracy. The segmentation error was found to be three times
lower than the current clinical standards.
  We also found that our method can successfully segment tumors of varying
lengths, anatomies and imaging qualities, as demonstrated by the high DICE scores
for different length bins of the esophageal tumor. Our future work includes
investigating if and to what extent the use of multi-modality imaging and
clinical history can improve the segmentation accuracy beyond what is achievable
by alone by using CT.

formation evaluation obtained by well-log interpretation while drilling. A
reliable, computationally efficient, and robust workflow to interpret well logs
and capture uncertainties in real-time is necessary for this application. An
iterative ensemble-based method, namely the approximate Levenberg Marquardt
form of the Ensemble Randomized Maximum Likelihood (LM-EnRML) is integrated in
our formation evaluation workflow. We estimate model parameters, resistivity
and density in addition to boundary locations, and related uncertainties by
reducing the statistical misfit between the measurements from the well logging
tools and the theoretical measurements from the forward tool simulators. The
results of analyzing several synthetic cases with several types of logs
verified that the proposed method can give good estimate of model parameters.

about 10--125 times lower computational time compare to a common statistical
method, such as Metropolis-Hastings Monte Carlo. In addition, the
ensemble-based method can run in parallel on multiple CPUs. Testing the method
on a case inspired from a real field also yielded accurate formation
evaluation. Thus, we conclude that the proposed method can be used to achieve
geological parameters in real-time well logging interpretation.

can provide diagnostic tools for interpreters to assess the consistency of the
theoretical measurements with the measurements from the well logging tools.

one of core knowledge
extraction techniques, named entity recognition (NER) is widely used to extract
information from texts for downstream tasks. Nested NER is a branch of NER in
which the named entities (NEs) are nested with each other. However, most of the
previous studies on nested NER usually apply linear structure to model the
nested NEs which are actually accommodated in a hierarchical structure. Thus in
order to address this mismatch, this work models the full nested NEs in a
sentence as a holistic structure, then we propose a holistic structure parsing
algorithm to disclose the entire NEs once for all. Besides, there is no
research on applying corpus-level information to NER currently. To make up for
the loss of this information, we introduce Point-wise Mutual Information (PMI)
and other frequency features from corpus-aware statistics for even better
performance by holistic modeling from sentence-level to corpus-level.
Experiments show that our model yields promising results on widely-used
benchmarks which approach or even achieve state-of-the-art. Further empirical
studies show that our proposed corpus-aware features can substantially improve
NER domain adaptation, which demonstrates the surprising advantage of our
proposed corpus-level holistic structure modeling.

  Wireless sensor networks (WSNs) have numerous applications such as health and
engineering fields, military, environmental monitoring, biomedicine, and
robotics . In many of these applications , a central node (or anchor node)
needs to know the location of all the other nodes (or sensor nodes) . This
location information can be obtained by installing location information
capabilities at the sensor nodes , or by deploying a set of anchor nodes that
can determine the location of all sensor nodes . The latter is known as
range-based localization.
  The main objective of localization algorithms is to estimate the position of
a node based on the distance between that node and a set of known anchor
nodes. There are three main categories of range-based localization algorithms:
active, observable and cooperative . The active algorithms obtain the
position by measuring the distance between a node and a set of known anchors .
Examples of this category are Time Of Arrival (TOA), Time Difference Of Arrival
(TDOA), Round Trip Time (RTT) and Signal Strength Indicator (SSI) . The
observable category uses external nodes to calculate the position . An example
of this category is trilateration. The cooperative category assumes that the
nodes in the network can share information with each other to achieve better
accuracy . An example of this category is weighted least squares (WLS) .

we found that the circulation of misinformation could have been a localized
phenomenon per se, as 75% of all misinformation shares were determined by
within-state shares, with only 25% being due to inter-state shares. Together

propagation of misinformation should be studied as a spatial process, as

(some with multiple variants). We define some of Hypatia's exotic cones, and
for conic constraints over these cones, we analyze techniques for constructing
equivalent representations using the standard cones. For optimization problems
from a variety of applications, we introduce natural formulations using these
exotic cones, and we show that the natural formulations are simpler and
lower-dimensional than the equivalent extended formulations. Our computational
experiments demonstrate the potential advantages, especially in terms of solve
time and memory usage, of solving the natural formulations with Hypatia

solver will encourage future developers to implement cones that are tailored to

preprocessing steps and tested the pipeline with and without them. We further

distributions of the models without preprocessing trained on ABIDE and CATI
data. Our main results were that a model using features extracted from MRIQC
without preprocessing yielded the best results when trained and evaluated on

heterogeneous population, such as the CATI dataset, provides the best scores on

the release of the Intel Optane DC Persistent Memory Module (or just "Optane DC
PMM"). This new nonvolatile DIMM supports byte-granularity accesses with access
times on the order of DRAM, while also providing data storage that survives
power outages. This work comprises the first in-depth, scholarly, performance
review of Intel's Optane DC PMM, exploring its capabilities as a main memory
device, and as persistent, byte-addressable memory exposed to user-space
applications. This report details the technologies performance under a number
of modes and scenarios, and across a wide variety of macro-scale benchmarks.
Optane DC PMMs can be used as large memory devices with a DRAM cache to hide
their lower bandwidth and higher latency. When used in this Memory (or cached)
mode, Optane DC memory has little impact on applications with small memory
footprints. Applications with larger memory footprints may experience some
slow-down relative to DRAM, but are now able to keep much more data in memory.
When used under a file system, Optane DC PMMs can result in significant
performance gains, especially when the file system is optimized to use the
load/store interface of the Optane DC PMM and the application uses many small,
persistent writes. For instance, using the NOVA-relaxed NVMM file system, we
can improve the performance of benchmarks by up to 15x, but only if the file
system is optimized to use the write interface of the Optane DC PMM. If the
file system is not optimized for this device, then we may even see poor
performance relative to DRAM. Finally, we explore the performance of a
microbenchmark that measures the ability of an application to make persistent
changes to data in memory. This microbenchmark shows that the Optane DC PMM
returns our results to DRAM after a power cycle, but only for the data that
were modified and only if the application had a valid checkpoint before the
power cycle. If the power cycle happens while the memory is mapped into the
address space of a process, then all data in that memory will be returned to
the original state. If the memory is not mapped into the address space of a
process at the time of the power cycle, then some data may be lost. If the
power cycle happens before a checkpoint can be written, then some data may
be lost as well.

In this paper, we consider the multi-agent extension of the Motivation Dynamics
framework and show how the framework can be extended to encode persistent
multi-agent rendezvous behaviors. We analytically characterize the bifurcation
properties of the resulting system, and numerically show that it exhibits
complex recurrent behavior suggestive of a strange attractor.
  We then show how this complex behavior can be exploited to create a
bifurcation-based decision-making system capable of learning from experience.
Specifically, we show that the system can use recurrent behavior to
leveraging short-term feedback to recover from long-term failures, and that it
can use bifurcations to deliberately change its behavior in response to
deteriorating sensing conditions. Finally, we show that the resulting system
can improve its navigation performance relative to a benchmark method, and that
it can adapt to changing sensing conditions to improve its ability to detect
and respond to other agents.
  Our work has the potential to create autonomous mobile agents that can
learn to perform recurrent multi-agent rendezvous behaviors and adapt to
degrading sensing conditions. As such, it has the potential to improve the
effective operating time of mobile agents relative to a baseline approach, and
to address multi-agent search and rescue applications.

efficient collection protocol for Wireless Sensor Networks. The former is the
Bidirectional Link Quality Estimation, which allows nodes to easily and quickly
compute the quality of a link between a pair of nodes. The latter, Hierarchical
Range Sectoring, organizes sensors in different sectors based on their location
within the network. Based on this organization, nodes from each sector are
coordinated to transmit in specific periods of time to reduce the hidden
terminal problem. To evaluate these two mechanisms, a protocol called HBCP
(Hierarchical-Based Collection Protocol), that implements both mechanisms, has
been implemented in TinyOS 2.1, and evaluated in a testbed using TelosB motes.
The results show that the HBCP protocol is able to achieve a very high
reliability, especially in large networks and in scenarios with bottlenecks.
Moreover, it is able to balance the energy consumption among the nodes,
preventing some nodes from dying before the rest. The HBCP protocol is able to
achieve an efficiency close to the optimal in most scenarios, except for the
bottleneck scenarios.

estimation, Sectoring

featuremap (two-stage methods) and full context without any cropping

each deep detector category. We create a fully controlled dataset for varying
context and investigate the context for deep detectors. We also evaluate
gradually removing the background context and the foreground object on MS COCO.

use the context by virtue of their large receptive field. Thus, choosing the
best object detector may depend on the application context.
  We provide a new perspective on object detector comparison and demonstrate
that choice of object detector is tied to the context of the image. Piston
design, where the best object detector is chosen for a specific application,
is proposed as a viable alternative to object detector design.
  We provide a simple framework for measuring the context effect on the test
data and demonstrate that popular evaluation metrics such as mAP@FLIP and
mAP@Hard may not effectively measure the context effect.
  We present a new metric, average intersection over union along the
segregation boundary, to measure the context effect and demonstrate that
comparison of object detectors on natural datasets such as COCO is more
effective when considered from the perspective of varying context.

context effect on object detectors.

a major barrier in kidney
transplantation (KT). The increasing shortage of kidney donors has driven the
development of desensitization techniques to overcome this immunological
challenge. Compared with compatible KT, patients undergoing incompatible KTs
are more likely to experience rejection, infection, malignancy, and graft loss.

end-stage kidney disease patients. To capture the effect of incompatibility, we
propose a Markov Decision Process (MDP) model that explicitly includes
compatibility as a state variable. The resulting higher-dimensional model makes
it more challenging to analyze, but under suitable conditions, we derive
structural properties including control limit-type optimal policies that are
easy to compute and implement. Numerical examples illustrate the behavior of
the optimal policy under different mismatch levels and highlight the importance
of explicitly incorporating the incompatibility level into the acceptance
decision when desensitization therapy is an option.

list. The goal is to maximize the total utility, which includes the quality of
the kidneys accepted and the compatibility of the kidneys accepted. To model
the waitlist inequality, we introduce a bias into the compatibility state
variable. Numerical examples illustrate the substantial impact of waitlist
inequality on the total utility and highlight the importance of addressing
inequality in organ allocation policies.

and propose strategies to improve compatibility through desensitization therapy.

provide a framework for investigating other transplant organs.

complexity lower bound showing the sharpness of our guarantees.

probabilities of action profiles are easy to communicate and implement, yet

of CCE, where players are allowed to form coalitions and negotiate over

systematics like undetected companions and to consider other tests like the

of gravity. However, because wide binaries reflect the local stellar density
profile, which is strongly affected by the galaxy's mass distribution, it is
a difficult problem to disentangle from the mass of the galaxy.

measurements of the cosmic microwave background. For each of these
applications, a better understanding of the statistics of polarization in
relation to source characteristics is crucial. In this paper, we derive the
median fractional polarization, $\Pi_{0, \rm med}$, of large samples of radio
sources with 1.4 GHz flux density $6.6 < S_{1.4} < 70$ mJy, by stacking 1.4 GHz
NVSS polarized intensity as a function of angular size derived from the FIRST
survey. Five samples with deconvolved mean angular size 1.8" to 8.2" and two
samples of symmetric double sources are analyzed. These samples represent most
sources smaller than or near the median angular size of the mJy radio source
population We find that the median fractional polarization $\Pi_{0,\rm med}$ at
1.4 GHz is a strong function of source angular size less than ~5" and a weak
function of angular size for larger sources up to ~8". We interpret our results
as depolarization inside the AGN host galaxy and its circumgalactic medium.
Assuming magnetic field scale size of 4 kpc and 1 kpc for sources larger than
or smaller than ~4", respectively, we use the median polarization to place
limits on the spin temperature of the cosmic web, the warm/hot gas within the
host galaxy. We obtain lower limits of 2.9 x 10$^{6}$ K and 3.0 x 10$^{7}$ K,
respecting previous estimates. These limits will be improved by analyzing
sources at other frequencies.
  Based on the analysis of mJy radio sources, we estimate that AGN-powered
radio sources as a whole are missing a global polarization budget of $\sim$
17% - 25% due to intrinsic polarization and that of an even larger sample of
lower flux density sources will be necessary to fully represent the population
of AGN-powered radio sources.
  We also find that symmetric double sources have a different polarization
physics than the single doubles in our sample and that their polarization
properties are more similar to the largest sources in our sample.

  We propose that sudden, super-Eddington mass ejections from massive stars are
not restricted to the usual core collapse scenario, but also can result from
the collapse of their surrounding envelope. This idea is based on a central
explosion that generates a pressure wave with enough energy to drive a strong
shock. The critical distinction between this proposal and previous ideas about
the importance of pressure waves in massive star evolution is that the wave's
energy is not radiated or dissipated, but instead is retained and concentrated
by the star's increasing mass. We demonstrate that this idea is valid for a
range of initial envelope densities and that the resulting shocks can be
dominated by internal heat sources.

between a central explosion and its surrounding envelope in a massive star. We
describe the initial conditions based on a parametrized density profile and

envelope. We demonstrate that the exchange of mass and momentum between the
explosion products and the envelope is critical to determining the outcome of
the interaction. In particular, whether the envelope collapses or is ejected,
and the mass in the resulting star or supernova. We propose that the retention
of mass by the star is equivalent to, and an important component of, the core
mass function.

They have a wide range of applications and are often visualized as a 2-layered
drawing, where each set of objects is visualized as a set of vertices (points)
on one of the two parallel horizontal lines and the relationships are
represented by edges (simple curves) between the two lines connecting the
corresponding vertices. One of the common objectives in such drawings is to
minimize the number of crossings this, however, is computationally expensive
and may still result in drawings with so many crossings that they affect the
readability of the drawing. We consider a recent approach to remove crossings
in such visualizations by splitting vertices, where the goal is to find the
minimum number of vertices to be split to obtain a planar drawing. We show that
determining whether a planar drawing exists after splitting at most $k$
vertices is fixed parameter tractable in $k$.
  Furthermore, we introduce two new measures for the quality of a drawing,
generalizing the concept of crossings to simple curves (edges) that are not
horizontal. We investigate the complexity of determining the minimum number of
vertices to be split to obtain a drawing with zero crossings and, for the two
new measures, the minimum number of vertices to be split such that the number
of crossings per edge does not exceed 1 and the number of crossings per
visualization (per edge as well as per curve) does not exceed 2. Last, we
introduce a new simplification of these problems, where the splitting of
vertices is restricted to one of the two sets of objects. We provide exact and
parameterized algorithms and lower bounds for the decision and search
variants.
  We also introduce a new game called Curve Cover, where players compete in
placing curves to cover a set of points. We show that this game extends
fundamentally the known literature, as it introduces a genuine competitive
aspect, where the placement of curves by one of the two players, typically
disrupts the optimal coverage by the other player. We investigate basic

change on knot diagrams. Any knot diagram
can be transformed into a trivial unknot diagram by a series of unknotting
operations plus some Reidemeister moves. Unknotting operations have significant
importance in knot theory; they are used to study the complexity of knots and
invariants of knots. Unknotting operations are also important in biology,
chemistry, and physics to study the sophisticated entanglements of strings,
organic compounds, and DNA. In this paper, we introduced a new unknotting
operation called the diagonal move for classical and welded knots. We show that
the crossing change, Delta-move, Sharp-move, Gamma-move, n-gon move, pass move,
and 4-move can be realized by a sequence of diagonal moves. We also define the
distance induced by the diagonal move and study its properties.
  Suppose $K$ can be obtained from $J$ by a sequence of diagonal moves, then
$\delta(J,K)\leqslant b(J,K)^2$ and $\delta(J,K)=\varphi(b(J,K),K)$. We also
show that the distance $\delta$ is well-defined on the set of classical knots
within the bound of 12. We also give upper bounds for the distance $\delta$,
and we relate $\delta$ to other knot invariants such as the bridge index, the
minimal crossling number, and the volume of a knot.
  Finally, we introduce a new invariant of welded knots called the cut distance
$\delta_c$. We study properties of $\delta_c$, and we show that
$\delta_c(J,K)\geqslant b_c(J,K)$ for any classical knot $J$ and welded knot
$K$.
  A natural extension of the diagonal move to links is an extended diagonal
move. We study the extended diagonal move, and we show that the crossing change
and the n-gon move can be realized by a sequence of extended diagonal moves. We
also give an operation on colored knots and colored links.
  Finally, we study a game called the knot game. We give a set of rules for the
game, and we relate the game to the distance $\delta$ and the cut distance
$\delta_c$.

privacy-preserving learning paradigm that allows
multiple parities to jointly train a powerful machine learning model without
sharing their private data. According to the form of collaboration, FL can be
further divided into horizontal federated learning (HFL) and vertical federated
learning (VFL). In HFL, participants share the same feature space and
collaborate on data samples, while in VFL, participants share the same sample
IDs and collaborate on features. VFL has a broader scope of applications and is
arguably more suitable for joint model training between large enterprises.
  In this paper, we focus on VFL and investigate potential privacy leakage in
real-world VFL frameworks. We design and implement two practical privacy
attacks: reverse multiplication attack for the logistic regression VFL
protocol; and reverse sum attack for the XGBoost VFL protocol. We empirically
show that the two attacks are (1) effective - the adversary can successfully
steal the private training data, even when the intermediate outputs are
encrypted to protect data privacy; (2) evasive - the attacks do not deviate
from the protocol specification nor deteriorate the accuracy of the target
model; and (3) easy - the adversary needs little prior knowledge about the data
distribution of the target participant. We also show the leaked information is
as effective as the raw training data in training an alternative classifier. We
further show that the logitic regression leak is remediable by using encrypted
element-wise product. We highlight the necessity of securing VFL from privacy
leakages of intermediate outputs, protocol design, and practical
settings.
  We also investigate challenges and solutions from the perspective of
developers who build VFL frameworks. We emphasize the need of collaboration
between developers and users (data owners) to establish trust. We propose some
solutions based on technical aspects (e.g., secure multi-party computation and
homomorphic encryption), and social ones (e.g., auditability and coercion
resistance). We highlight the necessity of developing trustworthy VFL frameworks
that can fulfill the requirements of both computational power and transparency.
We also emphasize the need of research in this direction.
  In conclusion, our work investigates potential privacy leakage in real-world
VFL frameworks. It highlights the necessity of securing VFL from privacy
leakages, and calls for collaboration between developers and data owners to
establish trust. It also emphasizes the need of defining standards and best
practices for VFL frameworks.

large scale datasets by approximating kernel function using randomized Fourier

datasets. In this paper, we propose a kernel approximation method in a data

number of feature dimensions and also to improve the prediction performance.

  Let $G$ be a finite group, ${\mathbb P}(X)$ the power set of $X$. For $Y
\in {\mathbb P}(X)$ $G$ acts on $Y$ by $gy = \{g(a) : a \in y\}$ for all $g \in
G$ and $y \in Y$. Such an action is called a permutation action. The group
acting regularly is those that are isomorphic to $G$ itself.
  Let $x \in X$. The stabilizer of $x$ is
$$
  S_x = \{g \in G : gx = x\}.
$$
  When $S_x = \{e\}$, it is said that $G$ acts regularly on the set $X$.
  A diagonal group $D_A(G)$ is the subgroup of the wreath product $G^X$ by
Aleshitz theorem that
$$
  D_A(G) \cong (A \vee S_A(G)) / S_A(G),
$$
where $A$ is a complemented subgroup of $G$, $S_A(G)$ the core of $A$ and
$\vee$ the join of groups.
  In Section 2, we show how a group acting regularly is embedded into the
wreath product in the product action. In Section 3, we show how a diagonal
group is embedded into the wreath product in the product action.
  Finally, in Section 4, we give necessary conditions for a subgroup to be
a diagonal subgroup of $G$.

valve replacement
surgery in patients with the congenital heart disease Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF)
is mainly based on ventricular volume and function according to current
guidelines. Both of these two biomarkers are most reliably assessed by
segmentation of 3D cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) images. In several grand
challenges in the last years, U-Net architectures have shown impressive results
on the provided data. However, in clinical practice, data sets are more diverse
considering individual pathologies and image properties derived from different
scanner properties. Additionally, specific training data for complex rare
diseases like TOF is scarce.
  For this work, 1) we assessed the accuracy gap when using a publicly
available labelled data set (the Automatic Cardiac Diagnosis Challenge (ACDC)
data set) for training and subsequent applying it to CMR data of TOF patients
and vice versa and 2) whether we can achieve similar results when applying the
model to a more heterogeneous data base.
  Multiple deep learning models were trained with four-fold cross validation.
Afterwards they were evaluated on the respective unseen CMR images from the
other collection. Our results confirm that current deep learning models can
achieve excellent results (left ventricle dice of
$0.951\pm{0.003}$/$0.941\pm{0.007}$ train/validation) but also show that the
accuracy greatly decreases when applying the model to a different data base (dice
of $0.476\pm{0.103}$/$0.467\pm{0.099}$ train/validation).
  In a second step we could also show that the models can generalize better when
more of the CMR images are included in the training data, but also that the
generalization performance is worse compared to training and evaluating on the
same data base.
  We conclude that while deep learning models can process 3D CMR images, they
need to be trained on a large amount of data from the specific disease group of
interest and also that more effort has to be put into creating labelled data
bases.
  Finally, we want to stress that that our results also emphasize the importance
of an appropriate analysis of the images before applying a segmentation model,
as misleading results may occur when not accounting for the lack of generalization
in applications.

implicitly define extreme dependencies. It is easy to implement algorithms to
fit such models and evaluate the extremal characteristics of the data using

properties of the data using monte carol methods.

samples. We show that we can capture different implicit dependencies on the
extremes in different regions of Europe by specifying separate hidden states

the performance of Informed OCR or
iOCR. iOCR was developed with a spell correction algorithm to fix errors
introduced by conventional OCR for vote tabulation. The results found that the
iOCR system outperforms conventional OCR techniques.
  From a technical standpoint, iOCR represents a particular implementation of
a more general iOCR framework. This framework represents iOCR as a
learning-based postprocessing step for correcting the errors introduced by
conventional OCR techniques, rather than as a replacement for conventional
OCR. With this mindset, the iOCR system could be replaced with any other
learning-based postprocessing step to correct OCR errors.
  In contrast, the particular spell-check postprocessing step in the iOCR
system was carefully designed to match the shape and orientation of the
written text it seeks to correct. The resulting iOCR performance is thus tied
to the particular write styles found in the ballot papers it is used to tabulate
and may not be optimal for write styles found in other contexts.
  To illustrate this point, the conventional OCR step in the iOCR framework
could be replaced with a learning-based alternative without modifying the
informed nature of the correction step. Conversely, the informed nature of the
iOCR system reflects the particular learning strategy it employs - a
spelling-check postprocessing step adapted to write styles in South Africa. It
may not be optimal for write styles in other countries.
  With this in mind, the purpose of this paper is to explore the performance of
iOCR across various vote sheets. The results found show that iOCR outperforms
conventional OCR techniques.
  The rest of this report is organized as follows. Section II describes the

temperature near the critical one. The fixed point behavior is also appeared in
the temperature dependence of normalized factorial cumulants at least from the
fourth-order one. With a mapping from the Ising model to QCD, the fixed point
behavior is also found in the energy dependence of the normalized cumulants (or
fourth-order factorial cumulants) along different freeze-out curves.
  Therefore, the fixed point behavior of the cumulants of the order parameter
in the Ising model, as a representative of the universality class of QCD, is
found both at the critical temperature and in finite-size systems. The
experimental data of the normalized cumulants of particle ratio distributions
from the beam energy scan program at STAR experiment are also analyzed. The
theoretical values of the cumulants from the Ising model can well reproduce the
experimental data including the fluctuations of the binding energy of the
hadrons. The binding energy fluctuation may be an indicator of the critical
region. The critical temperature of the system measured from the data may be
lower than the one calculated from non-perturbative relativistic viscous
hydrodynamics. Further theoretical and experimental studies are needed to
understand the particle number fluctuations in heavy-ion collisions.

perspective of the distribution width in the phase space is also discussed by
studying the temperature dependence of the variance of the order parameter in
the Ising model.

the Ising model, as a representative of the universality class of QCD, is

context of graph-structured data. We discuss the formulations of DP applicable
to the publication of graphs and their associated statistics as well as machine
learning on graph-based data, including graph neural networks (GNNs). The
formulation of DP in the context of graph-structured data is difficult, as
individual data points are interconnected (often non-linearly or sparsely).
This connectivity complicates the computation of individual privacy loss in
differentially private learning. The problem is exacerbated by an absence of a
single, well-established formulation of DP in graph settings. This issue
extends to the domain of GNNs, rendering private machine learning on
graph-structured data a challenging task. A lack of prior systematisation work
motivated us to study graph-based learning from a privacy perspective. In this
work, we systematise different formulations of DP on graphs, discuss challenges
and promising applications, including the GNN domain. We compare and separate
works into graph analysis tasks and graph learning tasks with GNNs. Finally, we
conclude our work with a discussion of open questions and potential directions
for further research in this area.

set of control points, we construct a parametric curve that represents a road
network, which defines the dynamic driving task an automated lane keep system
equipped vehicle has to perform. Changing control points has global influence
on the resulting road geometry. Our approach uses search to find a set of
control points that results in a challenging road geometry, eventually forcing
the vehicle to leave the intended path. We evaluated our approach in three
different search-configurations regarding test efficiency and practical
applicability for automatic virtual testing of an automated lane keep system.

resulting road geometries were too simple to challenge an automated lane keep
system. The other two search configurations produced more challenging road
geometries but at the cost of test efficiency. Regarding the balance between
test efficiency and practical applicability, the middle configuration seems to
be the best.

new stochastic hydrodynamic method for the description of interacting Bose
gases. It goes beyond existing hydrodynamic approaches, such as superfluid
hydrodynamics or generalized hydrodynamics, in its capacity to simulate the

non-equilibrium quantum correlations, even for short-wavelength phenomena.
Using this description, we derive a linearized stochastic hydrodynamic scheme
which is able to simulate such non-equilibrium situations for longer times than
the full positive-P approach, at the expense of approximating the treatment of
quantum fluctuations, and show that this linearized scheme can be directly
connected with existing Bogoliubov approaches. Furthermore, we go on to
demonstrate the usefulness and advantages of this formalism by exploring the
correlations that arise in a quantum shock wave scenario and comparing its
predictions to other established quantum many-body approaches.
  We find that the full positive-P method is able to capture the onset of
condensation in a expanding system, while the linearized scheme is able to
simulate long-time equilibration scenarios where the full positive-P approach
is unable to describe due to breakdown of the condensate phase. This work
provides a comprehensive overview of the positive-P formalism, as well as
deriving a useful stochastic hydrodynamic scheme capable of describing the
dynamics of weakly interacting Bose gases.

for non-holonomic robots
moving at constant linear speeds in the 2-D plane is considered. The maneuvers
to avoid collisions are designed using dynamic vortex potential fields (PFs)
and their negative gradients; this formulation leads to a reciprocal behaviour
between the robots, denoted as being cooperative. The repulsive field is
selected as a function of the velocity and position of a robot relative to
another and introducing vorticity in its definition guarantees the absence of
local minima. Such a repulsive field is activated by a robot only when it is on
a collision path with other mobile robots or stationary obstacles. By analysing
the kinematics-based engagement dynamics in polar coordinates, it is shown that
a cooperative robot is able to avoid collisions with non-cooperating robots,
such as stationary and constant velocity robots, as well as those actively
seeking to collide with it. Conditions on the PF parameters are identified that
ensure collision avoidance for all cases. Experimental results acquired using a
mobile robot platform support the theoretical contributions.
  A novel method for avoiding collisions between robots moving at constant
linear speeds is presented.
  The proposed approach uses dynamic potential fields (PFs) which are chosen to
favour a reciprocal behaviour between the robots, namely cooperation, as their
negatives.
  The repulsive field, activated by a robot in response to another on a collision
course, introduces vorticity, leading to the absence of local minima.
  By analysing the kinematics-based engagement dynamics in polar coordinates,
conditions on the PF parameters are identified that guarantee collision avoidance
for a cooperating robot, regardless of the relative dynamics with a non-cooperating
robot.
  Experimental evidence acquired using a mobile robot platform confirms the
theoretical contributions.
  The proposed approach is applicable to the collision avoidance of robots
moving at constant linear speeds in 2-D.
  It can also be extended to robots moving at different linear speeds by
introducing time-varying PFs.
  The extension to robots moving non-linearly is more challenging and requires
further investigation.
  In the case of robots moving non-linearly, the definition of a PF that
guarantees global convergence to a collision-free state is not straightforward.
  Such a challenge is currently being investigated using singular optimal control
theory.
  The results will be reported in a future paper.

has recently attracted a
lot of interest in wireless communications research. An IRS consists of passive
reflective elements capable of tuning the phase, amplitude, frequency and
polarization of the impinging waveforms. Given such desirable properties, the
wireless channel characteristics can be controlled and optimized for specific
signal design and processing needs -- thus promising significant potential in
radar applications. In this paper, we establish the theoretical foundations for
introducing IRS into a radar system and study the potential to improve target
parameter estimation. More specifically, we will investigate the deployment of
IRS in cases where the line-of-sight (LOS) link is weak or blocked by
obstructions. We demonstrate that the IRS can provide a virtual or
non-line-of-sight (NLOS) link between the radar and target leading to an
enhanced radar performance. The effectiveness of such an IRS-provided virtual
link in estimating the moving target parameters is illustrated under both
optimized and non-optimized IRS scenarios. Numerical simulations indicate that
the IRS can enhance the target parameter estimation when the LOS link is weaker
than $\sim 10^{-1}$ in relative strength in comparison with the NLOS link.
Additionally, the use of IRS can also improve the robustness of the radar
system to cases of large scattering targets, over-reliance on a single assisting
wireless channel, and arbitrary polarization of the transmitted signal.
Moreover, the IRS can improve a moving target's detectability even when its
speed is less than the worst-case speed readable by the radar system thanks to
the enhancement of the virtual link's data rate. The proposed IRS-based linking
scheme has the potential to improve the moving target parameter estimation
performance as well as other radar performance metrics.
  Which of these advantages are possible when the IRS is provided with a
multifunction waveform are also discussed and illustrated through numerical
examples.

analysis subsumes various coverage measures and provides a large and diverse

a popular method for estimating the true
performance of machine learning models, allowing model selection and parameter
tuning. However, the very process of CV requires random partitioning of the
data and so our performance estimates are in fact stochastic, with variability
that can be substantial for natural language processing tasks. We demonstrate
that these unstable estimates cannot be relied upon for effective parameter
tuning. The resulting tuned parameters are highly sensitive to how our data is
partitioned, meaning that we often select sub-optimal parameter choices and
have serious reproducibility issues.
  Instead, we propose to use the less variable J-K-fold CV, in which J
independent K-fold cross validations are used to assess performance. Our main
contributions are extending J-K-fold CV from performance estimation to
parameter tuning and investigating how to choose J and K. We argue that
variability is more important than bias for effective tuning and so advocate
lower choices of K than are typically seen in the NLP literature, instead use
the saved computation to increase J. To demonstrate the generality of our
recommendations we investigate a wide range of case-studies: sentiment
classification (both general and target-specific), part-of-speech tagging and
document classification.

considerably, while substantially improving our tuned parameters. We also find
that we can achieve similar results by choosing J and K optimally, although
the question of how to optimise these choices is still open.

architecture design, the quality of knowledge, and the theoretical studies of

professional knowledge work is
an understudied area. Here we investigate how public sector officials
self-assess their dependency on the Google Web search engine, whether they are
aware of the potential impact of algorithmic biases on their ability to
retrieve all relevant information, and how much relevant information may
actually be missed due to Web search personalisation. We find that the majority
of participants in our experimental study are neither aware that there is a
potential problem nor do they have a strategy to mitigate the risk of missing
relevant information when performing online searches. Most significantly, we
provide empirical evidence that up to 20% of relevant information may be missed
due to Web search personalisation. This work has significant implications for
Web research by public sector professionals, who should be provided with
training about the potential algorithmic biases that may affect their judgments
and decision making, as well as clear guidelines how to minimise the risk of
missing relevant information.

Function (ICCBF), as a method to synthesize safety-critical controllers for
non-linear control affine systems with input constraints. The method identifies
a subset of the safe set of states, and constructs a controller to render the
subset forward invariant. The feedback controller is represented as the
solution to a quadratic program, which can be solved efficiently for real-time
implementation. Furthermore, we show that ICCBFs are a generalization of Higher
Order Control Barrier Functions, and thus are applicable to systems of

cruise control problem, and a spacecraft rendezvous problem.
  We present a novel framework to address safety-critical control tasks that
require human intervention. Human operators provide safety-critical control
inputs to a robotic system, while the robotic system is controlled to
assure stability and performance. The key idea is to consider the human
operator as a unknown nonlinear actuator, and develop a control law to assure
global asymptotic stability of the overall system. We provide an
implementation of our approach on a satellite rendezvous scenario, where a
satellite tracks a target spacecraft under control inputs provided by a
human operator. We demonstrate that our approach allows the satellite to
assure global asymptotic stability, despite the uncertainty in the
nonlinearities introduced by the human operator.
  We present a novel method to synthesize safety-critical controllers for a
team of autonomous systems. The method defines a set of geometric constraints
among the systems, and represents these constraints as a rigid body graph. A
control law is defined to minimize relative motion among the bodies, while
minimizing the effect of faults on the overall motion. We represent the
fault-tolerant control as a sequence of reconfiguring scenarios, and define a
control law to reconfigure the team to achieve the desired task. We demonstrate
the effectiveness of our method for a team of underwater vehicles, and for a
team of orbiting satellites.

can communicate with the planet. Then, it develops a controller that uses the

also discover that the default significance level ($5$%) is too liberal when

Existing methods typically insert actors into the scene according to a set of
hand-crafted heuristics and are limited in their ability to model the true
complexity and diversity of real traffic scenes, thus inducing a content gap
between synthesized traffic scenes versus real ones. As a result, existing
simulators lack the fidelity necessary to train and test self-driving vehicles.
To address this limitation, we present SceneGen, a neural autoregressive model
of traffic scenes that eschews the need for rules and heuristics. In
particular, given the ego-vehicle state and a high definition map of
surrounding area, SceneGen inserts actors of various classes into the scene and
synthesizes their sizes, orientations, and velocities. We demonstrate on two
large-scale datasets SceneGen's ability to faithfully model distributions of
real traffic scenes. Moreover, we show that SceneGen coupled with sensor
simulation can be used to train perception models that generalize to the real
world.

clouds, hosting a super star cluster ($\sim5.6\times10^5$M$_{\odot}$), grain

over a period of 2Myr. The model also suggests that in the case of superbubbles

of ground-state wavefunctions associated with different classical nuclear
coordinates. Our approach uses a classical neural network to convert the
nuclear coordinates of a molecule into quantum parameters of a variational
quantum circuit. The model is trained using a fidelity loss function to
optimize the neural network parameters. We show that gradient evaluation is
efficient and numerically demonstrate our method's ability to prepare

very high overlap with the groundstates in practice. From a theoretical
perspective, we further prove limitations on these protocols by showing that if
we were able to learn across an avoided crossing using a small number of
samples, then we would be able to violate Grover's lower bound. Additionally,
we prove lower bounds on the amount of quantum data needed to learn a single
parameter and provide a heuristic for extending this to the number of parameters

of this work, including dynamical processes and molecular energy alignment.

on laparoscopic liver surgery, where we register the organ model obtained from
a preoperative CT scan to the intraoperative partial organ surface,
reconstructed from the laparoscopic video. This is a challenging task due to
sparse and noisy intraoperative data, real-time requirements and many unknowns

correspondences between pre- and intraoperative data can be extremely difficult
since the liver usually lacks distinct surface features and the used imaging
modalities suffer from very different types of noise. In this work, we train a
convolutional neural network to perform both the search for surface
correspondences as well as the non-rigid registration in one step. The network
is trained on physically accurate biomechanical simulations of randomly
generated, deforming organ-like structures. This enables the network to
immediately generalize to a new patient organ without the need to re-train. We
add various amounts of noise to the intraoperative surfaces during training,
making the network robust to noisy intraoperative data. During inference, the
network outputs the displacement field which matches the preoperative volume to
the partial intraoperative surface. In multiple experiments, we show that the
network translates well to real data while maintaining a high inference speed.

optimized to have minimal correspondence error for randomly translating
surfaces to each other. By jointly training the correspondence field estimation

One of the major obstacles that have historically delayed large scale adoption

have recently achieved remarkable performance running more bio-realistic
Spiking Neural Networks at high throughput and very low power consumption
making them a natural alternative to ANNs. Here, we propose using the Random
Neural Network (RNN), a spiking neural network with both theoretical and
practical appealing properties, as a general purpose classifier that can match
the classification power of ANNs on a number of tasks while enjoying all the
features of a spiking neural network. This is demonstrated on a number of
real-world classification datasets.

for high-dimensional data through pseudo-dimensional reduction. However, a
systematic comparison to ANNs on a number of datasets has not been reported
yet. Although the RNN learns a piece-wise linear classifier, we show that it
can classify a number of datasets with non-linear structure such as the
fashion version of the popular MNIST dataset and the Street View House Number
(SVHN) dataset.

learning, and show that it can improve its classification performance on some
datasets even without dimensionality increase through competitive learning.
Competitive learning is a neural learning algorithm that is fundamentally
different from the standard learning algorithm for the RNN and shares some
broad features with some modern deep learning algorithms.

outperforms the RNN on some datasets significantly while retaining all the
desirable features of the RNN. The CaRNN is presented as a simple motivation

current state-of-the-art deep learning models.

defines a general purpose classifier that can be used on a number of real-world

Las Vergnas and H\"{a}ggkvist, combines three well-studied properties of
graphs, namely matchings, Hamiltonicity and edge-colourings. In this work, we
study these concepts for cubic graphs in an attempt to characterise those cubic
graphs for which every perfect matching corresponds to one of the colours of a
proper 3-edge-colouring of the graph. We discuss that this is equivalent to
saying that such graphs are even-2-factorable (E2F), that is, all 2-factors of
the graph contain only even cycles. The case for bipartite cubic graphs is
trivial, since if $G$ is bipartite then it is E2F. Thus, we restrict our
attention to non-bipartite cubic graphs. A sufficient, but not necessary,
condition for a cubic graph to be E2F is that it has the PMH-property. The aim
of this work is to introduce an infinite family of E2F non-bipartite cubic
graphs, whose 2-factors we describe explicitly. We do this by introducing a
new construction of Hamiltonian cycles using what we call a `rotating
perfect matching'. We show that this construction leaves exactly one perfect
matching out, which is also shown to be compatible with one of the colours of
a proper 3-edge-colouring of the graph. This confirms a conjecture of H\"{a}ggkvist.

an even number greater than 3.

the Strong Perfect Graph Theorem, repeated degrees in 2-factors and the Harary-Miller conjecture.

learning system call filtering policies for containerized microservices
applications. At run-time, Timeloops automatically learns which system calls a
program should be allowed to invoke while rejecting attempts to call spurious
system calls. Further, Timeloops addresses many of the shortcomings of
state-of-the-art static analysis-based techniques, such as the ability to
generate tight filters for programs written in interpreted languages such as
PHP, Python, and JavaScript. Timeloops has a simple and robust implementation
because it is mainly built out of commodity, and proven, technologies such as
seccomp-BPF, systemd, and Podman containers, with fewer than 500 lines of code.
We demonstrate the utility of Timeloops by learning system calls for individual
services and two microservices benchmark applications, which utilize popular
technologies like Python Flask, Nginx (with PHP and Lua modules), Apache
Thrift, Memcached, Redis, and MongoDB. Further, the amortized performance of
Timeloops is similar to that of an unhardened system while producing a smaller
system call filter than state-of-the-art static analysis-based techniques.
Finally, Timeloops produces a system call filter that is compatible with
seccomp-based mandatory access control policies, enabling administrators to
combine the benefits of MC (Mission Critical) security with that of container
technology.

smart or careless action in critical
situations can change the result of the match. Therefore players, coaches, and
scouts are all curious about the best action to be performed in critical
situations, such as the times with a high probability of losing ball possession
or scoring a goal. This work proposes a new state representation for the soccer
game and a batch reinforcement learning to train a smart policy network. This
network gets the contextual information of the situation and proposes the
optimal action to maximize the expected goal for the team. We performed
extensive numerical experiments on the soccer logs made by InStat for 104
European soccer matches. The results show that in all 104 games, the optimized
policy obtains higher rewards than its counterpart in the behavior policy.
Besides, our framework learns policies that are close to the expected behavior
in the real world. For instance, in the optimized policy, we observe that some
actions such as foul, or ball out can be sometimes more rewarding than a shot
in specific situations.
  We also observe that the expected quality of the optimized policy can
considerably change with a few new training experiences. This indicates that
the optimization of the expected quality with respect to the log distribution
of one soccer game might not be feasible. Instead, our framework learns a
performance-sensitive state representation and a dataset of the best policies
for each possible situation independent of the log distribution. With more
logs, our framework can generate a richer set of policies. Besides, our state
representation and data-driven approach make it easier to train and evaluate
different network architectures, as we do not need to experience the large
variance of different matches.
  Finally, we highlight that the training of the policy might require an
extensive time computationally as well as conceptually (considering the
complexity of the soccer game). Therefore, we propose a "hybrid learning"
framework that learns a sub-policy for a fixed state representation once a
deep learning policy has been trained. The hybrid learning framework trains a
much faster policy than the one reported in this work. Besides, the learned
policy by the hybrid learning framework has similar rewards to the fully learned
policy in many cases.

study the joint effect of
immigration and a competition-dispersal tradeoff in the dynamics of two species
competing for space in regular lattices. Individuals of one species can invade
a nearest-neighbor site in the lattice, while individuals of the other species
are able to invade sites at any distance but are less competitive locally,
i.e., they establish with a probability $g \le 1$. The model also accounts for
immigration, modeled as an external noise that may spontaneously replace an
individual at a lattice site by another individual of the other species. This
combination of mechanisms gives rise to a rich variety of outcomes for species
competition, including exclusion of either species, mono-stable coexistence of
both species at different population proportions, and bi-stable coexistence
with proportions of populations that depend on the initial condition.
Remarkably, in the bi-stable phase, the system undergoes a discontinuous
transition as the intensity of immigration overcomes a threshold, leading to a
half loop dynamics associated to a cusp catastrophe, which causes the
irreversible loss of the species with the shortest dispersal range.
Quasi-stationary distribution and survival exponents are also studied for this
model.
Interestingly, an adequate selection of parameters leads to results that are
consistent with the Field of Flowers model's biological diversity-range
relationship.
Finally, the analysis of the model's asymmetry reveals a correlation between
the excess of asymmetry and the degree of diversity that the system is able to
support.
Detailed results are presented for up to $2.5 \times 10^7$ sites.
Simulation results are validated with a rigorous analysis of the quasi-stationary
distribution.
We also provide a detailed explanation of the discontinuous transition and its
consequences for species competition.

We propose a new neural network architecture to solve the sign problem. The
method can be used for any neural network, but specifically we are trying to
solve the sign problem for monte carlo simulations using neural networks. The
specific implementation we are presenting is for a particular setup, but the
general idea can be adapted to suit different situations. In brief, we are
combining two established methods: neural networks for monte carlo and
Lattice gauge theories. The architecture consists of multiple layers that
perform a particular operation on the complex-valued vectors that represent the
configuration variables of the lattice gauge theory. The operation is a
rotation which has a positive determinant, thus resolving the sign problem
inherent to the lattice gauge theories that we are currently applying this to.
Resolving the sign problem allows us to simulate larger volumes than was
previously possible, and to obtain results with smaller errors. We have
applied our method to the 2d QCD studies of the deconfinement phase transition,
where it has given results consistent with the signs problem free results, but
with the additional benefit of being able to study the dynamics out of the
equilibrium. We have also simulated larger volumes of the SU(2) gauge theory,
where we have found agreement with the sign problem free results for the
string tension, and have shown that the perturbative result for the gap
filling factor is reproduced at moderate volumes.

health and social stability. At present, understanding and curbing the spread

mechanism and propose a method to quantify a rumors' influence by the speed of
new insiders. The search frequency of the rumor is used as an observation
variable of new insiders. The peak coefficient and the attenuation coefficient
are calculated for the search frequency, which conforms to the exponential
distribution. We designed several rumor features and used the above two
coefficients as predictable labels. A 5-fold cross-validation experiment using
the mean square error (MSE) as the loss function showed that the decision tree

outbreak coefficient, while location information and rumor entity information

Finally, we discuss how to use deep learning technology to reduce the forecast
loss by combining the predicted coefficients, and a variant of the long short

effectively reduced.

(PNe) offer a way to determine the distance
to their host galaxies thanks to the nearly universal shape of the planetary
nebulae luminosity function (PNLF). Accurate PNe distance measurements rely on
obtaining well-sampled PNLFs and the number of observed PNe scales with the
encompassed stellar mass. This means either disposing of wide-field
observations or focusing on the bright central regions of galaxies. In this
work we take this second approach and conduct a census of the PNe population in
the central regions of galaxies in the Fornax cluster, using VLT/MUSE data for
the early-type galaxies observed over the course of the Fornax3D survey. Using
such integral-field spectroscopic observations to carefully separate the
nebular emission from the stellar continuum, we isolated [OIII] 5007 {\AA}
sources of interest, filtered out unresolved impostor sources or kinematic
outliers, and present a catalogue of 1350 unique PNe sources across 21
early-type galaxies, which includes their positions, [OIII] 5007 {\AA} line
magnitudes, and line-of-sight velocities. Using the PNe catalogued within each
galaxy, we present independently derived distance estimates based on the fit to
the entire observed PNLF observed while carefully accounting for the PNe
detection incompleteness and uncertainty in the measured magnitudes. We
validate the reliability of these distance estimates by deriving a scatter of
just 0.12 dex when comparing them to previous distance measurements based on
other methods for the 10 galaxies for which such comparisons are possible. We
furthernote that the PNe line-of-sight velocity distributions offer a way to
assess the motion of the galaxy within the cluster, with a median Fornax
cluster velocity of 1401.1 $\pm$ 1.0 km/s (standard error) based on early-type
galaxies, in excellent agreement with the previously published cluster velocity
value. Finally, we present the preliminary results of an analysis of the
relationship between the PNe luminosity function shape and galaxy mass,
highlighting the need for a thorough statistical investigation once more PNe
sources are catalogued.

evaluation methodology. Our evaluation shows that Labs reduces the
development-to-evaluation time by an order of magnitude.

methodology and implementation of a high-performance stream processing engine

neural network. Many loss functions have been designed to date, making a
correct choice nontrivial. However, elaborate justifications regarding the
choice of the loss function are not made in related work. This is, as we see
it, an indication of a dogmatic mindset in the deep learning community which
lacks empirical foundation. In this work, we consider deep neural networks in a
supervised classification setting and analyze the impact the choice of loss
function has onto the training result. While certain loss functions perform
suboptimally, our work empirically shows that under-represented losses such as
the KL Divergence can outperform the State-of-the-Art choices significantly,
highlighting the need to include the loss function as a tuned hyperparameter
rather than a fixed choice.
  Which losses should be considered is left as open research, as the space of
possible choices is infinite. To facilitate research, we make \textit{LossLand}
a available repository, comprising a containerized framework to train neural
networks with a wide array of choices regarding the activation functions, the
optimizer, and the loss function. The framework is designed to be lightweight
and cross-language compatible, utilizing the \textit{LightXML} library for
convenient configuration and the \textit{OpenBLAS} library for speed-critical
matrix operations. With \textit{LossLand}, we present a systematic empirical
analysis regarding the effectiveness of various losses, highlighting the
loss function as a critical component in the pipeline rather than a fixed
choice.
  Finally, we release \textit{LossLand}'s benchmark results, containing a
comprehensive empirical analysis regarding the impact the choice of loss function
has onto the training result, which might be a valuable reference for researchers
in the field.
