chanical modeling of the
strain-induced crystallization in unfilled polymers. This phenomenon
significantly influences mechanical and thermal properties of polymers and has
to be taken into consideration when planning manufacturing processes as well as
applications of the final product. In order to simultaneously capture both
kinds of effects, the model proposed starts by introducing a triple
decomposition of the deformation gradient and furthermore uses thermodynamic
framework for material modeling based on the Coleman--Noll procedure and
minimum principle of the dissipation potential, which requires suitable
assumptions for the Helmholtz free energy and the dissipation potential. The
chosen setup yields evolution equations which are able to simulate the
formation and the degradation of crystalline regions accompanied by the
temperature change during a cyclic tensile test. The boundary value problem
corresponding to the described process includes the balance of linear momentum
and balance of energy and serves as a basis for the numerical implementation
within an FEM code. The~paper closes with the numerical examples showing the
microstructure evolution and temperature distribution for different material
samples.

calculate the Zeeman part of magnetic susceptibility for nematic and chiral
superconducting phases near T$_c$ in Ginzburg-Landau formalism. Superconducting
order parameter from $E_u$ representation has non-trivial coupling with the
transversal Zeeman field that results in a paramagnetic response to a
magnetization. The topology of a Fermi surface has a strong influence on

eventually leads to phase transition from the nematic to chiral phase. At the
transition point, magnetic susceptibility diverges. Also, we study the effects
of the electron-electron interaction on the competition between nematic and
chiral phases. We found that in a real system, electron-electron interaction

difficulty of requiring optimal state action demonstrations limits the space of
problems where the teacher can provide quality feedback. As an alternative to
state action demonstrations, the teacher can provide corrective feedback such

learn from specific types of noisy feedback, but across teachers and tasks
different forms of feedback may be required. Instead we propose that in order
to learn from a diversity of scenarios we need to learn from a variety of
feedback. To learn from a variety of feedback we make the following insight:
the teacher's cost function is latent and we can model a stream of feedback as
a stream of loss functions. We then use any online learning algorithm to
minimize the sum of these losses. With this insight we can learn from a
diversity of feedback that is weakly correlated with the teacher's true cost
function. We unify prior work into a general corrective feedback meta-algorithm
and show that regardless of feedback we can obtain the same regret bounds. We
demonstrate our approach by learning to perform a household navigation task on
a robotic racecar platform. Our results show that our approach can learn to
perform a task after receiving only a few interactions per trial.

Let $f:(0,1)^d\rightarrow \mathbb{R}^d$ be the function that sends each $x$
to the point at distance $|x_x|$ from the origin, where $|x_x|$ is defined by
$|x_x|^d = \prod_{i=1}^d (1-x_i)$. The function $f$ is well known to
represent the Minkowski gauge with respect to the unit cube
$\{(x_1,\ldots,x_d): 0<x_i<1, \forall i\}$, that is the shortest distance to this
unit cube measured from any point $y\in \mathbb{R}^d$. It is well known that
for all points $y\in \mathbb{R}^d$ we have $f(y/||y||_{\infty}) \rightarrow
\pm y$ as $\|y\|_{\infty} \rightarrow \infty$. This observation has led Farris
to construct certain interesting polyhedra. We observe that $f$ does not
preserve directions. We demonstrate this by showing that the limit of
$f(y/||y||_1) $ does not give a multiple of $y$ when $\|y\|_1 \rightarrow \infty$.
We also show that $f$ does not give a scaling of the input vector when
$\|y\|_2 \rightarrow \infty$. We observe that the failure of $f$ to preserve
directions might be useful in constructing polyhedra.

polyhedra in $\mathbb{E}^d$. We then apply this algorithm to construct a new
polyhedron in the euclidean space $\mathbb{E}^3$.

Broadbent and Lord (TQC'20), is an
encryption scheme with the following attractive feature: given a ciphertext, an
adversary cannot create two ciphertexts both of which decrypt to the same
message as the original ciphertext. We revisit this notion and show the
following:
  - Reusability: The constructions proposed by Broadbent and Lord have the
disadvantage that they either guarantee one-time security (that is, the
encryption key can only be used once to encrypt the message) in the plain model
or they guaranteed security in the random oracle model. We construct unclonable
encryption schemes with semantic security. We present two constructions (for
public-key and private-key settings) from minimal cryptographic assumptions.
  - Lower Bound and Generalized Construction: We revisit the
information-theoretic one-time secure construction of Broadbent and Lord. The
success probability of the adversary in their construction was guaranteed to be
$0.85^n$, where $n$ is the length of the message. It was interesting to
understand whether the ideal success probability of (negligibly close to)
$0.5^n$ was unattainable. We generalize their construction to be based on a
broader class of monogamy of entanglement games. We demonstrate a simple
cloning attack that succeeds with probability $0.71^n$ against a class of
schemes built using this framework. We also construct a simple information
theoretically secure unclonable encryption scheme with a higher success
probability ($0.84^n$) and which also offers more cryptographic features
(such as public-key setting and forward security).
  - Quantum Resistant Construction: All constructions presented so far were
based on conventional cryptographic assumptions which are now being
challenged by the rise of quantum computers. We construct unclonable encryption
schemes using (post-quantum) key agreement protocols to guarantee quantum
resistance. We also construct simple unclonable encryption schemes from
quantum-key-distribution (QKD) protocols. While these constructions guarantee
quantum resistance, the key exchange in these constructions is restricted to
the sub-family of QKD based schemes which, despite their beautiful
experimental realizations, have not yet gained popularity in the classical
communication setting (due to their stringent requirements) and are mainly
used in the experimental setting.

driven by line-scattering of the star's radiative momentum, while in the Sun
and even lower-mass stars a much weaker mass loss arises from the thermal
expansion of a mechanically heated corona. In exoplanets around such low-mass
stars, the radiative heating and wind interaction can lead to thermal expansion
or mechanical ablation of their atmospheres. Stellar magnetospheres result from
the internal trapping of the wind outflow, while planetary magnetospheres are
typically shaped by the external impact from the star's wind. But in both cases

signatures such as X-ray flares and radio outbursts. This review will aim to
give an overview of the underlying physics of these processes with emphasis on
their similarities and distinctions for stars vs. planets.

evidence for thermal expansion from the expansion of the heated atmosphere.

generate the wind and how the magnetic stress from the external wind shapes

neural networks with respect to their inputs. To this end, we provide a simple
technique for computing an upper bound to the Lipschitz constant---for multiple
$p$-norms---of a feed forward neural network composed of commonly used layer
types. Our technique is then used to formulate training a neural network with a
bounded Lipschitz constant as a constrained optimisation problem that can be
solved using projected stochastic gradient methods. Our evaluation study shows
that the performance of the resulting models exceeds that of models trained
with other common regularisers. We also provide evidence that the
hyperparameters are intuitive to tune, demonstrate how the choice of norm for
computing the Lipschitz constant impacts the resulting model, and show that the
performance gains provided by our method are particularly noticeable when only
a small amount of training data is available.
  Which norm is the best for computing the Lipschitz constant of a neural
network? This question is left to the practitioner, and may depend on the
dataset at hand. We provide evidence that the choice of norm has a non-trivial
impact on the performance of the resulting model, and to help answer this

environments and robot kinematics/dynamics, recent works on constrained

choice settings, we explore its usefulness in tackling various combinatorial
optimization problems. We do so by considering an abstract model, in which a
set of agents are asked to act in a particular ordering, called the action
sequence. Each agent acts in a way that gives her the maximum possible value,
given the actions of the agents who preceded her in the action sequence. Our
goal is to compute action sequences that yield approximately optimal total
value to the agents (a.k.a., social welfare). We assume query access to the
value $v_i(S)$ that the agent i gets when she acts after the agents in the
ordered set $S$.
  We establish tight bounds on the social welfare that can be achieved using
polynomially many queries. Even though these bounds show a marginally sublinear
approximation of optimal social welfare in general, excellent approximations
can be obtained when the valuations stem from an underlying combinatorial
domain. Indicatively, when the valuations are defined using bipartite
matchings, arborescences in directed graphs, and satisfiability of Boolean
expressions, simple query-efficient algorithms yield $2$-approximations. We
discuss issues related to truthfulness and show how some of our algorithms can
be implemented truthfully using VCG-like payments. Finally, we introduce and
study the price of serial dictatorship, an innovation cost measure of
social welfare that reflects the limited power of the agents in restoring
optimal social welfare through strategic action.

study within the Strongly Rational Social Welfare (SRSW) framework that we
propose. Within SRSW, we study pure and mixed strategies of agents, we discuss
issues related to truthfulness and mechanism design, and we define social
welfare bounds in terms of the valuations' complexity.

  We propose a novel unsupervised pre-training framework for medical
segmentation, which avoids the drawback of contrastive learning.
  Our framework consists of two principles: unsupervised over-segmentation as a
pre-train task using mutual information maximization and boundary-aware preserving
learning.
  Experimental results on two benchmark medical segmentation datasets reveal our
method's effectiveness in improving segmentation performance when few annotated
images are available.
  Furthermore, our method outperforms contrastive learning in terms of easing
overfitting when only a small amount of labeled data is available (few-shot
setting).
  The proposed method sets a new baseline for unsupervised pre-training in medical
segmentation, and it has the potential to be extended to other segmentation
domains.

super-oversegmentation (over-oversegmentation) results due to the complete
ignoration of spatial context, and we illustrate its practical effects on

universe, known as early dark
energy (EDE), is a proposed solution to the Hubble tension. Currently, there is
no consensus in the literature as to whether EDE can simultaneously solve the
Hubble tension and provide an adequate fit to the data from the cosmic
microwave background (CMB) and large-scale structure of the universe. In this
work, we deconstruct the current constraints from the Planck CMB and the
full-shape clustering data of the Baryon Oscillation Spectroscopic Survey
(BOSS) to understand the origin of different conclusions in the literature. We
use two different analyses, a grid sampling and a profile likelihood, to
investigate whether the current constraints suffer from volume effects upon
marginalization and are biased towards some values of the EDE fraction,
$f_\mathrm{EDE}$. We find that $f_\mathrm{EDE}$ allowed by the data strongly
depends on the particular choice of the other parameters of the model and that
several choices of these parameters prefer larger values of $f_\mathrm{EDE}$
than in the Markov Chain Monte Carlo analysis. This suggests that volume
effects are the reason behind the disagreement in the literature. Motivated by
this, we use a profile likelihood to analyze the EDE model and compute a
confidence interval for $f_\mathrm{EDE}$, finding $f_\mathrm{EDE} \le 0.23$ at
$95.4\%$ confidence. Furthermore, we show that $f_\mathrm{EDE}$ is strongly
correlated with the present Hubble parameter, $H_0$, and that the proposed
solution to the Hubble tension, $f_\mathrm{EDE} \simeq 0.14$, may not be
compatible with the CMB data if we constrain $H_0$ to its precise value as
measured by local distance indicators.
  We also investigate the effect of adding EDE to the $\Lambda$CDM model on
the basis of the Hubble main sequence, finding that EDE is not capable of
describing the whole Hubble sequence, and that some parameters may be
contaminated by systematic errors. Finally, we derive a constraint on
$f_\mathrm{EDE}$ from the observed value of the Hubble parameter, finding
$f_\mathrm{EDE} < 0.26$ at $68\%$ confidence.

wearable devices such as
smart phones and wristbands make it easy to get access to people's health
information including activities, sleep, sports, etc. Smart healthcare achieves
great success by training machine learning models on a large quantity of user
data. However, there are two critical challenges. Firstly, user data often
exists in the form of isolated islands, making it difficult to perform
aggregation without compromising privacy security. Secondly, the models trained
on the cloud fail on personalization. In this paper, we propose FedHealth, the
first federated transfer learning framework for wearable healthcare to tackle
these challenges. FedHealth performs data aggregation through federated
learning, and then builds personalized models by transfer learning. It is able
to achieve accurate and personalized healthcare without compromising privacy
and security. Experiments demonstrate that FedHealth produces higher accuracy
(5.3% improvement) for wearable activity recognition when compared to
traditional methods. FedHealth is general and extensible and has the potential
to be used in many healthcare applications.
  We propose FedHealth, the first federated transfer learning framework for
wearable healthcare.
  The key component in FedHealth is a novel federated transfer learning
algorithm, which achieves accurate and personalized healthcare without
compromising privacy and security.
  Experiments demonstrate that FedHealth produces higher accuracy (5.3% improvement) for
WearActivityRecognition when compared to traditional methods.

signal the beginning of the end of our universe, perhaps even through
decompactification, with possible implications for the cosmological coincidence
problem. Thanks to the scarcity (absence?) of stable de Sitter vacua, dark
energy in string theory is assumed to take the form of a quintessence field in
slow roll. As it rolls, a tower of heavy states will generically descend,
triggering an apocalyptic phase transition in the low energy cosmological
dynamics after at most a few hundred Hubble times. As a result, dark energy
domination cannot continue indefinitely and there is at least a percentage
chance that we find ourselves in the first Hubble epoch. We use a toy model of
quintessence coupled to a tower of heavy states to explicitly demonstrate the
breakdown in the cosmological dynamics as the tower becomes light. This occurs
through a large number of corresponding particles being produced after a
certain time, overwhelming quintessence. We also discuss some implications for
early universe inflation.
  We show that a first "dark energy transition" of order a billion years is
predictively possible if the transition is driven by the production of
heavy states. This would explain the observed present day value of the state
of dark energy, without the need for slow roll for an aesthetically
undesirable million billion years. We also propose that if the tower does not
signal the beginning of the end of our universe, it may instead lead to a
conjecture connecting the maximum value of the cosmological constant to the
minimum value of the energy density in the early universe.
  Finally, we discuss the possibility that the apocalyptic phase transition
could be connected to the origin of the first stars.

This problem studies the model where the same sequence from some set is
transmitted over multiple channels, and the decoder receives the different
outputs. Assume that the transmitted sequence is at distance $d$ from some code
and there are at most $r$ errors in every channel. Then the sequence
reconstruction problem is to find the minimum number of channels required to
recover exactly the transmitted sequence that has to be greater than the
maximum intersection between two metric balls of radius $r$, where the distance
between their centers is at least $d$. In this paper, we study the sequence
reconstruction problem of permutations under the Hamming distance. In this
model, we define a Cayley graph and find the exact value of the largest
intersection of two metric balls in this graph under the Hamming distance for
$r=4$ with $d\geqslant 5$, and for $d=2r$.
  We also study the sequence reconstruction problem of permutations under the
Hamming distance when the number of errors is bounded by $r_1, r_2,...,r_\ell$
along the channels. In this model, we define a certain covering in which the
hamming balls of radius $r_i$ are included, to find the minimum number of
channels needed to recover exactly the transmitted sequence: $\ell$ is the
minimum number of channels such that the hamming balls of radius $r_\ell$ cover
the entire set of permutations, provided that $d\geSLant \sum_{i=1}^\ell r_i$.
Finally, we study the sequence reconstruction problem of permutations under the
Hamming distance when the number of errors along the channels is bounded by
$r_1,r_2,...,r_\ell$ and there is a significant amount of noise in the source
that transmits the sequence. In this model, and under the assumption that the
source is stable, we find the maximum intersection of two metric balls along
which the Hamming distance between their centers is at least $d$, for different
values of $d$ and $r_i$.

is important in many
applications, including flood risk management. The shallow water equations
(SWEs) are commonly used for this purpose. However, traditional numerical
solvers of the SWEs are computationally expensive and require high-resolution
riverbed profile measurement (bathymetry). In this work, we propose a two-stage
process in which, first, using the principal component geostatistical approach
(PCGA) we estimate the probability density function of the bathymetry from flow
velocity measurements, and then use machine learning (ML) algorithms to obtain
a fast solver for the SWEs. The fast solver uses realizations from the
posterior bathymetry distribution and takes as input the prescribed range of
BCs. The first stage allows us to predict flow velocities without direct
measurement of the bathymetry. Furthermore, we augment the bathymetry posterior
distribution to a more general class of distributions before providing them as
inputs to ML algorithm in the second stage. This allows the solver to
incorporate future direct bathymetry measurements into the flow velocity
prediction for improved accuracy, even if the bathymetry changes over time
compared to its original indirect estimation. We propose and benchmark three
different solvers, referred to as PCA-DNN (principal component analysis-deep
neural network), SE (supervised encoder), and SVE (supervised variational
encoder), where the last three solvers are types of ML algorithms that perform
both feature learning and prediction in a unified framework. We find that the
SVE solver is the best performer in terms of accuracy and computational time,
among the three. Finally, we study the effect of increasing the depth of the
river on the performance of the solvers and show how the general approach
proposed here can be used to obtain a solver for the 3D SWEs.

temperature-related phase distortion: (1) low-frequency phase distortions due
to gross temperature gradients, (2) high-frequency distortions caused by the
finite RF pulse duration, and (3) local distortions in the boundary region
between the bed and the tube wall. The first and last of these can be
effectively compensated for by means of a simple image processing routine, while
the latter can be circumvented by means of careful design of the experimental
setup. The compiled guidelines can be directly applied to the study of
reacting gas-solid systems and can help to increase the spatial and temporal
resolution of future MR thermometry studies.

spatial and temporal resolution of the temperature mapping.

computational time is not so clear, and the best approach is the BDDC in some

preconditioner is still a competitive option for cardiac mechanics, in spite of

order to make a final conclusion, we introduce a simple strategy that allows us

times similar in all the test cases, including the realistic electromechanical

classification accuracy. We argue that such an inability to model uncertainty

modeling of open-world uncertainty as the extra dimension. To unify the
learning of the original $K$-way classification task and the extra dimension

and moreover, theoretically prove that optimizing such an objective essentially
forces the extra dimension to capture the marginal data distribution. Extensive
experiments show that our approach, Energy-based Open-World Softmax

quantifies the amount of spatial entanglement between the two photons.

achieved in principle.

non-symmetric nature of the two-photon entanglement. Again, the enhancement of
the Fisher information can become divergent as the separation is reduced below
the Rayleigh criterion.

could be useful in tracing photon migrations around an effective beam
propagating from the source, thus allowing for spatial field reconstruction.

shift of the spectral peaks in the different colors to gain additional
information about the separation.

leading to regime shifts are highly desirable in population biology. In this
paper, a two-trophic ecosystem comprising of two species of predators,
competing for their common prey, with explicit interference competition is
considered. With proper rescaling, the model is portrayed as a singularly
perturbed system with fast prey dynamics and slow dynamics of the predators. In
a parameter regime near singular Hopf bifurcation, chaotic mixed-mode
oscillations (MMOs), featuring concatenation of small and large amplitude
oscillations are observed as long-lasting transients before the system
approaches its asymptotic state. To analyze the dynamical cause that initiates
a large amplitude oscillation in an MMO orbit, the model is reduced to a
suitable normal form near the singular-Hopf point. The normal form possesses a
separatrix surface that separates two different types of oscillations. A large
amplitude oscillation is initiated if a trajectory moves from the "inner" to
the "outer side" of this surface. A set of conditions on the normal form
variables are obtained to determine whether a trajectory would exhibit another
cycle of MMO dynamics before experiencing a regime shift (i.e. approaching its
asymptotic state). These conditions can serve as early warning signs for a
sudden population shift in an ecosystem.

common food source, e.g. a fungus. The plant and the fungus are nourished by

investigate the oscillatory behavior in a self-sustaining ecosystem with and

a key role in regulating the populations and thus maintaining the health of the
ecosystem.

recently seen increased popularity due to their simplicity, potential
performance efficiency, and low energy consumption. However, such protocols
result in memory instruction reordering, thus causing extra program behaviors
that are often not intended by the programmers. We propose a novel formal model
that captures the semantics of programs running under such protocols, and
features a set of fences that interact with the coherence layer. Using the
model, we design an algorithm to analyze the reachability and check whether a
program satisfies a given safety property with the current set of fences. We
describe a method for insertion of optimal sets of fences that ensure
correctness of the program under such protocols. The method relies on a
counter-example guided fence insertion procedure. One feature of our method is
that it can handle a variety of fences (with different costs). This diversity
makes optimization more difficult since one has to optimize the total cost of
the inserted fences, rather than just their number. To demonstrate the strength
of our approach, we have implemented a prototype and run it on a wide range of
examples and benchmarks. We have also, using simulation, evaluated the
performance of the resulting fenced programs.

performance of our methodology. The implementation has a user-friendly interface
and can be made available upon request. Based on our experiments, we propose a
heuristic fence insertion procedure which is more efficient than the
counter-example guided procedure but still guarantees correctness of the
program. This procedure has been incorporated into a commercial compiler and
has been shown to be viable in practice.

integrated inside modern systems (e.g., GPU, GPU-like devices, and SSDs). These
devices have different coherence protocols and fencing mechanisms. To utilize
these findings further, we have studied how the behavior of programs running
these accelerators can be affected by the coherence protocol and how it can
be optimized using our methodology. This has led us to a generic framework for
fence insertion that takes into account the specific coherence protocol of the
device. We have also investigated optimization opportunities which arise from
the specific protocol.

star-forming massive ($>10^{11}\,\rm M_{\odot}$) galaxies within the core of
the RO-1001 galaxy group at $\rm z=2.91$. Each of them displays kpc-scale
compact star-bursting cores with properties consistent with forming galaxy
bulges, embedded at the center of extended, massive stellar disks.

lopsided. Therefore, `outside-in' quenching is ongoing in the three group
galaxies. We propose an overall scenario in which the strong mass lopsidedness
in the disks (ranging from factors of 1.6 to $>$3), likely generated under the
effects of accreted gas and clumps, is responsible for their star-formation
suppression, while funnelling gas into the nuclei and thus creating the central
starbursts. The lopsided side of the disks marks the location of accretion
streams impact, with additional matter components (dust and stars) detected in
their close proximity directly tracing the inflow direction. The interaction
with the accreted clumps, which can be regarded as minor-mergers, leads the
major axes of the three galaxies to be closely aligned with the outer
Lyman-$\alpha$-emitting halo and the accreted clump that they are interacting
with. The present work unveils the role of major-axis lopsidedness as a driver
of quasi-major-mergers in the early universe.

cores, including their stellar and total population synthesis models,
psychophysical analysis of their attenuation curves, and estimation of their
circumstellar gas contents. The cores display highly extinguished, stellar
continua consistent with being composed by young ($\lesssim500$ Myr old)
stars, but with a peculiar age distribution. The attenuation curves, as
measured through psychophysical analysis, are consistent with those produced by
circumstellar gas, and the gas masses are correlated with the star-formation
rates. The cores do not contain gas at the sensitivity limit of our data, but
their gas content suggests they have not yet completed their star-burst phase.
Furthermore, the stellar ages suggest they have ages ranging from $\sim150$
Myr to $\lesssim100$ Myr

deep anomaly detection methods are not designed to cope with, such as
conceptual drift and continuous learning. State-of-the-art flow anomaly

court compel the respondent to enter that password into the device? In this
work, we propose a new approach to the foregone conclusion doctrine from Fisher
v US that governs the answer to this question. The Holy Grail of this line of
work would be a framework for reasoning about whether the testimony implicit in
any action is already known to the government. In this paper we attempt
something narrower. We introduce a framework for specifying actions for which
all implicit testimony is, constructively, a foregone conclusion. Our approach
is centered around placing the burden of proof on the government to demonstrate
that it is not "rely[ing] on the truthtelling" of the respondent.
  Building on original legal analysis and using precise computer science
formalisms, we propose demonstrability as a new central concept for describing
compelled acts. We additionally provide a language for whether a compelled
action meaningfully entails the respondent to perform in a manner that is 'as
good as' the government's desired goal. Then, we apply our definitions to
analyze the compellability of several cryptographic primitives including
decryption, multifactor authentication, commitment schemes, and hash functions.
In particular, our framework reaches a novel conclusion about compelled
decryption in the setting that the encryption scheme is deniable: the
government can compel but the respondent is free to use this information for
anything except to transfer the encrypted data to the government.
  Can the government compel a respondent to perform a hash of some data? We
answer this question by asserting that the answer depends on the data. We
describe a dexterous response by a witness that minimizes the amount of work the
witness needs to do while still satisfying the hash query. We further show how
this approach can be used to optimize tasks involving cryptographic primitives
that can be used to simplify the task of which the hash is needed for.
  Finally, we study compelled password entry. We demonstrate that the
compellability of entering a password depends on the password entry interface.
We propose an alternative interaction that achieves the same goal with less
burden on the respondent.
  Our frameworks and results further illustrate the complexity of the foregone
conclusion doctrine. They emphasize the importance of a case-by-case analysis
of compelled acts and the need for technical tools that can assist the court in
reasoning about the doctrine.

to their unprecedented performance and high accuracy for different and
challenging problems of significant engineering importance. However, when such
deep learning architectures are utilized for making critical decisions such as
the ones that involve human lives (e.g., in control systems and medical
applications), it is of paramount importance to understand, trust, and in one
word "explain" the argument behind deep models' decisions. In many
applications, artificial neural networks (including DNNs) are considered as
black-box systems, which do not provide sufficient clue on their internal
processing actions. Although some recent efforts have been initiated to explain
the behaviors and decisions of deep networks, explainable artificial
intelligence (XAI) domain, which aims at reasoning about the behavior and
decisions of DNNs, is still in its infancy. The aim of this paper is to provide
a comprehensive overview on Understanding, Visualization, and Explanation of
the internal and overall behavior of DNNs.

understanding, visualization, and explanation of DNNs is reviewed. The most
popular techniques on feature learning are described and their applications are
listed. Finally, the paper is concluded in Section IV with a discussion on the
future directions for research in XAI.

internal behavior of deep models by using them for feature learning is

valley interference and dopant placement on the Heisenberg spin exchange
interaction. We find that the exchange can become immune to valley interference
by engineering in-plane dopant placement along specific crystallographic
directions. A vacuum-like behaviour is recovered, where the exchange is
maximised to the overlap between the donor orbitals, and pair-to-pair
variations limited to a factor of less than 10 considering the accuracy in
dopant positioning. This robustness remains over a large range of distances,
from the strongly Coulomb interacting regime relevant for high-fidelity quantum
computation to strongly coupled donor arrays of interest for quantum simulation
in silicon.

that are viable with state-of-the-art doping techniques. This work further

regions relevant to Parkinson's Disease based on local field potential data
collected from the brain of marmoset monkeys. Parkinson's disease is a
neurodegenerative disorder, linked to the death of dopaminergic neurons at the
substantia nigra pars compacta, which affects the normal dynamics of the basal
ganglia-thalamus-cortex neuronal circuit of the brain. Although there are
multiple mechanisms underlying the disease, a complete description of those
mechanisms and molecular pathogenesis are still missing, and there is still no
cure. To address this gap, computational models that resemble neurobiological
aspects found in animal models have been proposed. In our model, we performed a
data-driven approach in which a set of biologically constrained parameters is
optimised using differential evolution. Evolved models successfully resembled
single-neuron mean firing rates and spectral signatures of local field
potentials from healthy and parkinsonian marmoset brain data. As far as we are
concerned, this is the first computational model of Parkinson's Disease based
on simultaneous electrophysiological recordings from seven brain regions of
Marmoset monkeys. Results show that the proposed model could facilitate the
investigation of the mechanisms of PD and support the development of techniques
that can indicate new therapies. It could also be applied to other
computational neuroscience studies.
  We make two main contributions in this work. First, we propose a model of
Parkinson's Disease based on electrophysiological recordings from seven brain
regions of Marmoset monkeys. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first
computational model of PD based on data collected from Marmoset monkeys. It is
widely accepted that computational models developed from data collected from
Marmoset monkeys are more likely to lead to techniques that can be used in
human patients due to the similarities between the two species. Second, we
say that a data-driven approach reporting optimised parameters is often
required to evaluate the performance of a computational model of PD. Previous
works often compare the performance of computational models of PD by applying
synthetic lesions to a pre-trained model, and claiming that the output of the
model after lesions mimics the symptoms of PD, without providing evidence that
the model indeed captures the normal and parkinsonian dynamics of the basal
ganglia-thalamus-cortex neuronal circuit of the brain.

an approach to improving
the representation of convection in weather and climate models. This is an
attractive framework as it is fundamentally dynamical, removing some of the
assumptions of mass-flux convection schemes which are invalid at current model
resolutions. However, it is still not understood how best to close the
multi-fluid equations for atmospheric convection. In this paper we develop a
simple two-fluid, single-column model with one rising and one falling fluid. No
further modelling of sub-filter variability is included. We then apply this
model to Rayleigh-B\'{e}nard convection, showing that, with minimal closures,
the correct scaling of the heat flux (Nu) is predicted over six orders of
magnitude of buoyancy forcing (Ra). This suggests that even a very simple
two-fluid model can accurately capture the dominant coherent overturning
structures of convection.
  In contrast, a typical double-diffusive instability model (which is a
specific type of multi-fluid model and a inspiration for our approach) predicts
an order of magnitude error in the calculation of the Nusselt number at moderate
Rayleigh numbers. This suggests that these models are not yet suitable for
application to atmospheric convection where moderate-scale structures are
dominant. We also show that the combination of the falling fluid and the
removal of the assumption of statistical homogeneity lead to a suppression of
magnetic dynamo action in our two-fluid model, further suggesting that these
features are indeed important for modelling convection.
  Finally, we propose a simple extension of our two-fluid model that includes a
parameterisation of sub-filter variability, showing that this leads to results
that are consistent with direct numerical simulations of turbulent convection.
This suggests that this particular closure is able to accurately represent the
downscale enstrophy transfer in convective turbulence.
  These results further point to the potential of multi-fluid models to
represent convection properly, and highlight the need to carefully develop the
equations for the fluctuating variables.

Twitter provides organizations and
individuals an effective way to monitor public emotions towards them and their
competitors. As a result, sentiment analysis has become an important and
challenging task. In this work, we have collected seven publicly available and
manually annotated twitter sentiment datasets. We create a new training and
testing dataset from the collected datasets. We develop an LSTM model to
classify sentiment of a tweet and evaluate the model with the new dataset.
The experimental results show that the model is effective to classify twitter
sentiment.
  We have also applied the model to classify sentiment of tweets in a real
data dataset which is collected from Twitter for a set of keywords related to
the electric vehicle industry. The analysis provides insights into the public
experiences and opinions towards the electric vehicle industry. It also
demonstrates the effectiveness of sentiment analysis in real applications.

However, building a chat system is not scalable since it often requires a
considerable volume of human-human dialogue data, especially when enforcing
features such as persona, style, or safety. In this work, we study the
challenge of imposing roles on open-domain dialogue systems, with the goal of
making the systems maintain consistent roles while conversing naturally with
humans. To accomplish this, the system must satisfy a role specification that
includes certain conditions on the stated features as well as a system policy
on whether or not certain types of utterances are allowed. For this, we propose
an efficient data collection framework leveraging in-context few-shot learning
of large-scale language models for building role-satisfying dialogue dataset
from scratch. We then compare various architectures for open-domain dialogue
systems in terms of meeting role specifications while maintaining
conversational abilities. Automatic and human evaluations show that our models
return few out-of-bounds utterances, keeping competitive performance on general
metrics. We release a Korean dialogue dataset we built for further research.

The efficacies of pesticide
treatments are often evaluated by analyzing the average treatment effects and
risks. The stochastic efficiency with respect to a function is often employed
in such evaluations through ranking the certainty equivalents of each
treatment. The main challenge of using this method is gathering an adequate
number of observations to produce results with statistical power. However, in
many cases, only a limited number of trials are replicated in field
experiments, leaving an inadequate number of observations. In addition, this
method focuses only on the farmer's profit without incorporating the impact of
disease pressure on yield and profit. The objective of our study is to propose
a methodology to address the issue of an insufficient number of observations
using simulations and take into account the effect of disease pressure on yield
through a quantile regression model. We apply this method to the case of
strawberry disease management in Florida.
  For this study, we use a data set of combinations of yield and disease
severity from field experiments in Florida. We first fit a quantreg package
model to estimate the marginal effect of disease on yield at different
quantiles. We then simulate different scenarios of disease progression and
pesticide treatment efficacy to evaluate the performance of each treatment.
We find that the marginal effect of the disease on yield at the median is
consistent across simulations, while the average effect of the treatment on
profit and yield varies significantly across simulations, indicating a need for
more observations to produce reliable results. We recommend that future
research investigate management strategies that take into account the
quantifiable effects of disease pressure on yield.
  Finally, we suggest that farmers and agricultural consultants use a decision
support system that includes a disease growth model and a marginal product of
pesticide effectiveness to determine the optimal treatment strategy without
need for simulations.
  In conclusion, farmers and agricultural consultants who are managing the same
disease using similar agricultural practices can develop a model to estimate
the density of the pathogen and the likelihood of disease occurrence on their
fields. This model can assist them in deciding whether to apply a pesticide or
not based on the level of disease present and the benefit of treatment to the
crop. In addition, this model can help to evaluate the efficacy of a
pesticide treatment by estimating the density of the pathogen at the beginning
and end of the growing season. Finally, this model can assist farmers in
developing a management plan that includes best management practices such as
crop variety selection, pruning

$L(M)$ of a given module $M$. In \cite{St} R. P. Stanley outlined a method for
constucting a distributive lattice from a knowledge of its join irreducibles.
However it is not an easy task to identify all join irreducible submodules of a
given module. In the case of a multiplicity free module $M$ we present a
modifiiction of Stanley's method based on the composition factors of $M$. As
input we require a set of submodules $A_1,\ldots, A_n$ whose submodule
lattices are known and which contain all composition factors of $M$. From this
we can reconstruct $L(M)$. We illustrate the process for a family of Verma
modules $M(\gl_n)$, with $n $ a positive integer, for the Lie superalgebra
$\osp(3,2)$. We show that for $n\ge 2$, $L(M(\gl_n))$ is isomorphic to the
(extended) free distributive lattice of rank 3.
  As an application we present algorithms for such modules. We also outline
how the construction may be used to provide information on the value of
$\nu(M)$, the number of join irreducible submodules of $M$.
  Finally we introduce the notation $\lambda(L)$ (respectively $\nu(L)$) of a
lattice $L$ as the length of the longest descending chain of join irreducibles
in $L$ (respectively the number of join irreducibles in $L$). We define a
partial order, $\leq _\lambda$ (respectively $\leq _\nu$), on lattices as
$\lambda(L_1) \geq \lambda(L_2)$ if $L_1 \leq _\lambda L_2$ (respectively
$\nu(L_1) \geq \nu(L_2)$ if $L_1 \geq _\nu L_2$). We discuss the complexity
of determining $\lambda(M)$ and $\nu(M)$ for a given module $M$.
  We also investigate the value of $\lambda(L(M))$ for a modification of
Stanley's algorithm when applied to a module $M$ and we determine a lower
bound for this value in terms of some module homomorphisms from $M$.

decision problems restricted to some graph classes, deriving polynomial-time
algorithms, NP-completeness proofs, and initial parameterized complexity
results, including an answer to an open question in the literature for the
complexity of SG for chordal graphs.

parameterized algorithm for the class of chordal graphs, and a parameterized
proof for the exact-one parameterizer of the class of bipartite graphs. The
latter result confirms the following conjecture: all fixed-parameter
calculations for (SGR,SG) are feasible with a single parameter.

role of the Web as a driver of polarization. In order to further our
understanding of the factors behind online polarization, in the present work we
collect and analyze Web browsing histories of tens of thousands of users
alongside careful measurements of the time spent browsing various news sources.
We show that online news consumption follows a polarized pattern, where users'
visits to news sources aligned with their own political leaning are
substantially longer than their visits to other news sources. Next, we show
that such preferences hold at the individual as well as the population level,
as evidenced by the emergence of clear partisan communities of news domains
from aggregated browsing patterns. Finally, we tackle the important question of
the role of user choices in polarization. Are users simply following the links
proffered by their Web environment, or do they exacerbate partisan polarization
by intentionally pursuing like-minded news sources? To answer this question, we
compare browsing patterns with the underlying hyperlink structure spanned by
the considered news domains, finding strong evidence of polarization in
partisan browsing habits beyond that which can be explained by the hyperlink
structure of the Web.
  In this work we propose a novel measure of frozen polarization, i.e., the
portion of users who consistently pursue news sources aligned with their own
political leaning even when this requires leaving the hyperlink boundary of
their own web browsing community. We find that such frozen polarization is a
non-negligible fraction of all users, and that it is significantly more
prevalent than to what one would expect to explain overall polarization of
browsing patterns. Finally, we show that frozen polarization holds across
different Web domains, including both.com news sites and.org/nonprofit
domains, as well as across both the followed links as well as the explicitly
typed URLs.
  We conclude that while the following of frozen preferences is a prominent
factor behind polarization, it constitutes but a small fraction of all users
(around 5%). Instead, the vast majority of users (around 90%) exhibit
modifiable preferences, in the sense that their browsing habits can be
significant changed by simply not pursuing certain links. We expect that such
moduloing of preferences will be crucial in reducing the overall polarization of
the Web.

Numeration in base p/q is defined by a function
that evaluates each finite word over A_p={0,1,...,p-1} to some rational number.
We let N_p/q denote the image of this evaluation function. In particular, N_p/q
contains all nonnegative integers and the literature on base p/q usually
focuses on the set of words that are evaluated to nonnegative integers; it is a
rather chaotic language which is not context-free. On the contrary, we study
here the subsets of (N_p/q)^d that are p/q-recognisable, i.e. realised by
finite automata over (A_p)^d. First, we give a characterisation of these sets
as those definable in a first-order logic, similar to the one given by the
B\"uchi-Bruy\`ere Theorem for integer bases numeration systems. Second, we show
that the natural order relation and the modulo-q operator are not
p/q-recognisable.
  We also give necessary and sufficient conditions for a polynomial
p/q-recognisable set to be infinite, and we give examples of definable but
not p/q-recognisable sets.
  Finally, we investigate the closure properties of the class of
p/q-recognisable sets. In particular, we give sufficient conditions for the
Boolean operations and the unary successor to preserve it. We give counter
examples showing that in general it does not hold, but it does hold for
sets that are p/q-recognisable with error over a small finite set of words.
Finally, we study this last class of sets and we relate it to the class of
definable sets.

Edges and boundaries encode shape information, while textures manifest the
appearance of regions. Despite the success of Convolutional Neural Networks
(CNNs) in computer vision and medical image analysis applications,
predominantly only texture abstractions are learned, which often leads to
imprecise boundary delineations. In medical imaging, expert manual segmentation
often relies on organ boundaries; for example, to manually segment a liver, a
medical practitioner usually identifies edges first and subsequently fills in
the segmentation mask. Motivated by these observations, we propose a
plug-and-play module, dubbed Edge-Gated CNNs (EG-CNNs), that can be used with
existing encoder-decoder architectures to process both edge and texture
information. The EG-CNN learns to emphasize the edges in the encoder, to
predict crisp boundaries by an auxiliary edge supervision, and to fuse its
output with the original CNN output. We evaluate the effectiveness of the
EG-CNN with various mainstream CNNs on two publicly available datasets, BraTS
19 and KiTS 19 for brain tumor and kidney semantic segmentation. We demonstrate
how the addition of EG-CNN consistently improves segmentation accuracy and
generalization performance.
  We also conduct sensitivity analyses to probe the powers and limitations of
the proposed EG-CNN. While EG-CNNs excel for boundary-rich segmentation
domeains, they require large-scale edge annotations to be effective. We find
that the improvement in segmentation accuracy provided by EG-CNNs is directly
proportional to the size of the edge label space and that EG-CNNs are most
effective when compared to state-of-the-art non-edge based methods. To support
further investigation, we release the Brain tumor and Kidney Boundary
Databases, which contain manually delineated organ boundaries for the BraTS and
KiDS datasets.

transactional consistency protocols of MongoDB. Specifically, we provide a
concise pseudocode for the transactional consistency protocols in each MongoDB

evaluate efficient white-box checking algorithms for MongoDB transaction

Biases in the dataset can be learned by the model and degrade the
generalizability of the applications. There are studies on debiased models.
However, scientists and practitioners are difficult to identify implicit biases
in the datasets, which causes lack of reliable unbias test datasets to valid
models. To tackle this issue, we first define the data intrinsic bias
attribute, and then propose a novel bias identification framework for medical
image datasets. The framework contains two major components, KlotskiNet and
Bias Discriminant Direction Analysis(bdda), where KlostkiNet is to build the
mapping which makes backgrounds to distinguish positive and negative samples
and bdda provides a theoretical solution on determining bias attributes.
Experimental results on three datasets show the effectiveness of the bias
attributes discovered by the framework.
  We also find that in some cases the models trained by us have learned
implicit biases, and several popular unbias methods are tested to show the
effectiveness of our proposed bias attribute framework.

  Medical image analysis has achieved great progress with the help of deep
learning. However, there are cases that the models degrade significantly on
the real world data, different from the training datasets. There are many
reasons, such as the difference of patient demographics and the variations of
medical devices. One common method to improve the performance is to increase
the size of the training dataset by data augmentation. However, augmenting
medical images may increase the data intrinsic biases, e.g., the patient
age-based bias, and make models less robust to the new data.
  We propose a novel dataset processing framework, named COntrastive fRamework
for Reducing Data Intrinsic Bias (corfridb), to tackle this problem. It
contains two major components, the Contrastive Learning Framework (corf) and
the Bias Discriminant Direction Analysis (bddA). corf is to build the
contrastive mapping which makes backgrounds to distinguish positive and negative
samples and bddA provides a theoretical solution on determining bias attributes
that can improve or worsen the prediction accuracy of applications by
learning the common underlying medical anatomy, e.g., organ structures.

of such hybrid methods to global minimizers hinges on the discretization error
induced by restricting the discrete global optimization to the graph, with
corresponding implications on choosing an appropriate graph density. A prime
example is flight planning, i.e., the computation of optimal routes in view of
flight time and fuel consumption under given weather conditions. Highly
efficient discrete shortest path algorithms exist and can be used directly for
computing starting points for locally convergent optimal control methods. We
derive a priori and localized error bounds for the flight time of discrete
paths relative to the optimal continuous trajectory, in terms of the graph
density and the given wind field. These bounds allow designing graphs with an
optimal local connectivity structure. The properties of the bounds are
illustrated on a set of benchmark problems. It turns out that localization
improves the error bound by four orders of magnitude, but still leaves ample
opportunities for tighter error bounds by a posteriori estimators.
  We also apply the error bound to design a adaptive graph in a benchmark
problem motivated by airline network roadmapping. The adaptive graph yields a
discrete shortest path with a flight time only 1\% away from the optimal
continuous trajectory. At the same time the computation time is greatly
reduced: from approximately 54~minutes until the local minimum is found, to
less than 1~second up to the point where the error bound indicates that the

a multi-agent
system where a fraction of the agents act in an adversarial manner.
Specifically, the malicious agents steer the network of agents away from the
optimal solution by sending false information to their neighbors and consume
significant bandwidth in the communication process. We propose a distributed
gradient-based optimization algorithm in which the non-malicious agents
exchange quantized information with one another. We prove convergence of the
solution to a neighborhood of the optimal solution, and characterize the
solutions obtained under the communication-constrained environment and presence
of malicious agents. Numerical simulations to illustrate the results are also
presented.
  The paper is organized as follows. In Section II, we present the
formulation of the distributed optimization problem of interest. In Section III,
we propose the distributed gradient-based optimization algorithm for solving
the optimization problem under the communication-constrained environment and
presence of malicious agents. In Section IV, we prove convergence of the
solution to a neighborhood of the optimal solution under the communication-constrained
environment and presence of malicious agents. Numerical simulations to
illustrate the results are presented in Section V. We conclude our work in
Section VI.

the key probes of physical cosmology. The weak nature of this signal has driven
the construction of increasingly complex and sensitive experiments observing
the sky at multiple frequencies with thousands of polarization sensitive
detectors. Given the high sensitivity of such experiments, instrumental
systematic effects can become the limiting factor towards the full scientific
exploitation of their data. In this paper we present s4cmb (Systematics for
CMB), a Python package designed to simulate raw data streams in time domain of
modern CMB experiments based on bolometric technology, and to inject in these
realistic instrumental systematics effects. The aim of the package is to help
assessing the contamination due to instrumental systematic effects on real
data, to guide the design of future instruments, as well as to increase the
realism of simulated data sets required in the development of accurate data
analysis methods.
  We present a detailed description of the main components of the package,
including the demonstration of the integration with other popular tools in the
field, such as Camb and NumCosmo. This package is composed by independent
modules that can be easily customized to adapt to specific needs of different
users. For example, although we assume a bipolar nature for the DC drift
instrumental systematic, compatible with the design of the multi-layered
instruments like Keck Array and BICEP3, the package can be easily modified to
simulate other types of drift patterns, assuming instead a constant or linear
evolution, for example. Similarly, the package can be adapted to simulate the
instrumental systematics for optical systems, like the POLARBEAR experiment,
assuming a circular symmetry instead.
  Finally, we highlight that this package is designed to be user-friendly,
inclusively, with customizable parameters that can be adjusted to simulate a
wide range of scenarios compatible with the design and the observed
performance of real CMB experiments.

task, yet pre-trained language models have not been studied in word ordering,
let alone why they help. We use BART as an instance and show its effectiveness
in the task. To explain why BART helps word ordering, we extend analysis with
probing and empirically identify that syntactic dependency knowledge in BART is
a reliable explanation. We also report performance gains with BART in the
related partial tree linearization task, which readily extends our analysis.
## The Structure of BART in Word Ordering
We find BART's performance in word ordering to be closely tied to its
underlying structural knowledge of dependency parsing. First, BART outperforms
the baseline linear model on nearly all dependency types in the language (see
Table 3). Second, we observe that fine-tuning BART on a small dependency tree
generation dataset not only improves the baseline linear model but also
significantly the performance of a BART variant without pre-trained language
features (see Table 4). Third, we find that BART's performance in the tree
generation dataset is closely tied to its underlying structural knowledge of
dependency parsing.
## A Case Study with the Verb "printing"
To further examine how BART helps word ordering, we study one verb "printing"
in a synthetic context. We hypothesize that in this context, BART's
underlying structural knowledge of dependency parsing moderates the ordering of
words surrounding the verb "printing". We support this hypothesis by showing
that BART outperforms a linear model as well as a BART variant without
pre-trained language features. We also observe that the performance gap between
BART and the baselines increases with the distance to the verb "printing".
## Related Work
Both word ordering and partial tree linearization have been studied as
constrained language generation tasks taking unordered words as input. The
difference is that word ordering typically uses binary constraints while
partial tree linearization uses more general constraints including n-ary ones.

Here we propose a hybrid measurement attack, with only linear optics, homodyne
detection, and single photon detection, to the widely used vacuum+weak decoy
state QKD system when the phase of source is partially randomized. Our analysis
shows that, in some parameter regimes, the proposed attack would result in an
entanglement breaking channel but still be able to trick the legitimate users
to believe they have transmitted secure keys. That is, the eavesdropper is able
to steal all the key information without discovered by the users. Thus, our
proposal reveals that partial phase randomization is not sufficient to
guarantee the security of phase-encoding QKD systems with weak coherent states.
We also point out that the success of the proposed attack depends on the
strength of the phase randomization, and a fully phase randomized source would
force the users to use the rectangular basis set, which would then eliminate the
gap of channel parameters between the true and the simulated state, and thus
the security of the system would be restored.
  We would like to point out that the main purpose of our work is to propose a
particular hacking scheme for a particular QKD system, and it is not to
contributing to the development of new hacking techniques. Besides, as
discussed in the work, the proposed hacking scheme would not work if the source
is fully phase randomized. Thus, our proposal has already been partially
included in the recent comprehensive review on QKD hacking (see
G.P.Aprile et al., arXiv:2003.14567), and it is not necessary to have another
follow-up work to summarize the findings of the proposal. What we want to stress
again is that, despite the haking schemes proposed so far, the phase randomness
of the source is still not strongly regulated in current practical QKD systems,
and thus it is still important to have a fully phase randomized source in order
to guarantee the security of phase-encoding QKD systems.

angle function. He introduced a general definition of this notion for metric
and semi-metric spaces. He also proposed two problems concerning conformal
embeddability of spaces endowed with an angle function into Euclidean spaces.
These problems received attention in later years but only for some particular
cases of metric spaces. In this article we first update the definition of angle
function to apply to the larger class of spaces with a notion of betweenness,
which seem to us a more natural framework. In this new general setting, we
solve the two problems proposed by Menger.
  Another angle function, typically called metric of Hilbert, was introduced
in the early years of the twentieth century by D. Hilbert as a candidate for
an abstract metric function. We show that this metric also defines a system
of angle functions, and we use this observation to give a new solution to
Menger's problems.
  Finally, for the particular case of metric spaces we introduce the notion of
directly indecomposable angle function. This concept leads to interesting
examples and also allows to give yet another solution to Menger's problems.
  All these solutions have also been realized in the particular case of groups
with an angle function. It seems to us interesting to note that the main
arguments used in these solutions do not depend on the specific structure of
the spaces considered, and thus to apply to any space with an angle function.
  We also study the isoperimetric inequality of Menger's angle function, and
its relation with the direct indecomposability. In particular we show that in
some cases the minimum of Menger's angle function corresponds to the boundary
of a regular polygon.
  Finally, we study the angle function defined by the Hilbert metric, in the
particular case of subsets of $\mathbb{R}^2$. We also study, in the same
setting, the direct indecomposability and we give an isoperimetric inequality
which allows to characterize the subsets for which the angle function is
minimized.

solution seems to us to be close to the theory of groups with angle functions.

formation assumes that planetesimals
and planetary embryos are formed during the primordial, gaseous phases of the
protoplanetary disk. However, how the dust particles overcome the traditional
growth barriers is not well understood. The recently proposed viscous
ring-instability may explain the concentric rings observed in protoplanetary
disks by assuming that the dust grains can reduce the gas conductivity, which
can weaken the magneto-rotational instability. We present an analysis of this
model with the help of GPU-based numerical hydrodynamic simulations of coupled
gas and dust in the thin-disk limit. During the evolution of the disk the dusty
rings become Rossby unstable and break up into a cascade of small-scale
vortices. The vortices form secularly stable dusty structures, which could be
sites of planetesimal formation by the streaming instability as well as direct
gravitational collapse. The phenomenon of self-sustaining vortices is
consistent with observational constraints of exoplanets and sets a favorable
environment for planetary system formation.
  We find that the formation of dusty vortices is a realistic possibility
during the early transmission phase of the disk, when the temperature is
sufficiently high to prevent the dust grain freezing. However, the outcome of
the simulation depends strongly on the strength of dust gas friction. If this
friction is too weak the system enters a chaotic three-dimensional motion,
reminiscent of a dusty hydrodynamic earthquake. If it is too strong the dusty
rings become too narrow, and the system enters a state of turbulent chaotic
motion. Only intermediate friction values lead to self-sustaining dusty
whirlpools.
  Furthermore, we find that the formation of dusty vortices is also possible in
the extended protoplanetary phase, if the disk is externally heated by a host
star. However, in this case the dust grains are warmer than the gas, and the
different thermal velocities lead to a decoupling of the gas and dust phases
during the rotation of the vortices. This indicates that the formation of dusty
vortices is also possible in the extended planet formation phase, if the disk
is subject to external heating.
  Finally, we note that further investigations are required, as the models
presented above assume a vertically stratified disk. Furthermore, it remains an
open question, if the assumed dust grains with micron sizes are applicable to
the modeling of protoplanetary disks.

detect interstellar panspermia in even the nearest star clusters. Finally, we
note that even if microorganisms are incapable of surviving in interstellar

spacecraft. In this case, the prospects for detecting evidence of

designated as "high density" when, in truth, those areas are truly hotspots of
abundance. This last result has important implications for estimating population
size with SCR models, and suggests that SCR model estimates of density should
be interpreted as relative density across study sites, rather than absolute
density.

given an undirected graph
$G=(V,E)$ with edge costs $\{c_e:e \in E\}$. The goal is to find an edge set
$F\subseteq E$ that satisfies a prescribed property of minimum power
$p_c(F)=\sum_{v \in V} \max \{c_e: e \in F \mbox{ is incident to } v\}$. In the
Min-Power $k$ Edge Disjoint $st$-Paths problem $F$ should contains $k$ edge
disjoint $st$-paths. The problem admits a $k$-approximation algorithm, and it
was an open question whether it admits approximation ratio sublinear in $k$
even for unit costs. We give a $4\sqrt{2k}$-approximation algorithm for general
costs.
  Another variant of the problem is when we seek edge disjoint paths that
contain specific vertices in them. Min-Power $k$ Edge Disjoint $st$-Paths
contains this type of variants when all paths contain $s$ and $t$. In the
Min-Power $k$ Edge Disjoint $s-t$ Path problem $F$ should contains $k$ edge
disjoint $s-t$ paths. This problem admits a $2$-approximation algorithm, and
it was an open question whether its metric version admits approximation ratio
better than $2$. We prove that it does, by giving a $3/2$-approximation
algorithm for metric costs. All our algorithms extend to the variant when we
seek paths that contain specific vertices in them.
  Finally, we give polynomial-time constructions of lower bounds for the
approximation ratio of Min-Power $k$ Edge Disjoint $st$-Paths under various
restrictions on the cost function.

pre-planned mission and broadcast updates to a swarm of unmanned aerial
systems.

attempted is presented, and a simulation showing the effectiveness of this
method is provided.

the mission planning system and the swarm is described.

aspects of swarm mission planning and communication, as well as investigating a

inspecting their structure. We analyse eight of such methods and show that all
of them yield high polarization scores even for random networks with similar
density and degree distributions to typical real-world networks. Further, some

polarized groups. We propose normalization to the existing scores and a minimal
set of tests that a score should pass in order for it to be suitable for
separating polarized networks from random noise. The performance of the scores
increased by 38%-220% after normalization in a classification task of 203
networks. Further, we find that the choice of method is not as important as
normalization, after which most of the methods have better performance than the
best-performing method before normalization. This work opens up the possibility
to critically assess and compare the features and performance of different

introduce a new classification task for evaluating the performance of methods

being degree independent distinguishes $\Pi$ from other scores and allows it to
perform better on networks without strong clear-cut clusters. Further, a
classification task on 80 networks with clear-cut clusters shows that $\Pi$
performs comparable to other scores.

to testing of
programs. Their combination is intended to lead to benefits in reliable program
development, testing, and evolution. Our geometric theory of testing is
intended to serve as the specification of a testing environment, included as
the last stage of a toolchain that assists professional programmers, amateurs,
and students of Computer Science. The testing environment includes an automated
algorithm which locates errors in a test that has been run, and assists in
correcting them. It does this by displaying, on a monitor screen, a stick
diagram of causal chains in the execution of the program under test. The
diagram can then be navigated backwards in the familiar style of a satnav
following roads on a map. This will reveal selections of places at which the
program should be modified to remove the error.
  We describe the algorithm, the theory of causality which leads to the
construction of the diagram, and how it can be used to locate and correct errors
in a program. We do this by example of a scheme of implementing a traffic
light for a road which is not currently controlled by a standard traffic
light.
  We propose that a testing environment be included in a testing program, as
is done with checklists. The geometric algorithm could be automated still further
by making use of recent advances in the analysis of programs.
  This work develops and applies a formal theory of testing. It introduces a
new paradigm which can be used to improve the reliability of programs. It
defines a framework into which any formal program verification method can be
integrated. It suggests that complete formal verification might be replaced by
a sequence of partially formal tests.
  We argue that the geometric theory of testing should be given a standard
status within the Curricula of Computer Science.
  The geometric testing algorithm has been partially implemented in a testing
program, and has been used to test programs in a number of domains. The
implementation has led to the discovery of errors in the testing program,
particularly in the presentation of the diagram and in the navigation of it.
These are to be mended, and we welcome contributions from other practitioners.

beam dynamics as well as

longitudinal beam dynamics, including a discussion of possible dynamical
instabilities, will be presented. This will be accompanied by an explanation
of the mechanical design aspects of a circular machine and an discussion of

magnetic instabilities, resonances and magnet roll, beam-beam effects and
longitudinal instabilities.

electron cloud effect, collective instabilities (magnetic ripple and
electron-cloud ripple), coherent instabilities (land tunnelling, magnet roll

illustrated with examples from various circular machines.

presented and discussed with examples from various circular machines.

the COVID pandemic impacts
students' ability to keep up with the pace of instruction in a university level
physics course, with a focus on the heterogeneous impact of remote learning on
different demographic groups. Student learning data is collected from 70 online
learning modules assigned as both online homework and self-study material in
both Fall 2020 and Spring 2020 semesters, with the first 41 modules being
assigned before campus closure in Spring 2020. Students' ability to stay on
track is measured by three data indicators: percentage of modules submitted
before the due date, percentage of modules submitted early for extra credit,
and percentage of modules properly engaged with. The student population is
divided into two demographic groups according to each of the four demographic
variables: Gender, Ethnicity, Transfer Status and First generation status. All
three data indicators from both semesters are first compared between each pair
of demographic groups within the same semester, and then compared within the
same group between the two semesters. Exam and course scores are also compared
between demographics groups in Fall 2020 and against scores from the Fall 2019
semester. The analysis revealed that remote learning significantly reduced
on-time and early submission for first-generation students, but increased the
frequency of early submission for transfer students. Under-represented minority
students had higher percentage of engaged modules during the pandemic, while
non-URM students had a larger decrease. There was no significant change in any
indicator for both genders between Fall and Spring 2020, but women had a
significantly higher percentage of engaged modules in both semesters compared
to men.
  From a methodological perspective, this study highlights the advantages of
using learning data from 70 online learning modules to increase statistical
power when analyzing small demographic groups. It also illustrates how a
combination of three learning indicators can provide a more complete picture
of students' ability to keep up with the pace of instruction compared to a
single indicator.
  This article addresses the second research area of the COVID-19 Physics
Education Research Special Collection by investigating the impact of the
pandemic on student learning. It also begins to address the third research area
by investigating how different demographic groups are impacted differently.
Future work can investigate how demographic groups differ in their learning
outcomes, and how those differences can be predicted by various learning
indicators.

these decoders may yield decoding accuracies sufficient to safely operate

noise, previously known decoding algorithms, such as the bubble merging algorithm,
can be directly obtained via reinforcement learning, but there exist
significant opportunities for further improvement. In particular, we show that
there exist simple rules, which can be incorporated into the agent, that can
lead to an increase of 25% in success probability, 35% reduction in error
retirement per round, and significant improvement in code size.
  Furthermore, we show that the process of training a set of interacting decoding
agents, which can be thought of as a multi-agent learning problem, can also be
used to obtain logical gate operations, without the need for an a priori
implementation of such operations into the agents. We find that such a scheme
can lead to significant improvements in logical gate failure probabilities,
likely the most important and cost-effective of all near-term code implementations.
Finally, we show that the problem of repairing the code can also be naturally
incorporated into the agent, leading to further improvements in code performance.
All of the results reported in this work were obtained under the assumption of
faulty syndrome measurements, without any assumptions about the error modeling.
In particular, because of the diversity of errors that can occur, all of the
results reported in this work are for codes with error correction thresholds
significantly lower than what can be achieved under independent and identical
noise models.

deployment of HPC workloads on the best-fitting hardware. However, although
cloud and on-premise HPC systems offer similar computational resources, their
network architecture and performance may differ significantly. For example,
these systems use fundamentally different network transport and routing
protocols, which may introduce network noise that can eventually limit the
application scaling. This work analyzes network performance, scalability, and
cost of running HPC workloads on cloud systems. First, we consider latency,
bandwidth, and collective communication patterns in detailed small-scale
measurements, and then we simulate network performance at a larger scale. We
validate our approach on four popular cloud providers and three on-premise HPC
systems, showing that network (and also OS) noise can significantly impact
performance and cost both at small and large scale.
  We observe that cloud systems have higher network latency and bandwidth than
on-premise HPC systems, which can impact communication patterns used by
applications. To account for these differences, we integrate network performance
into the classification of communication-prone applications and evaluate it on
cloud and on-premise HPC systems. We find that cloud systems can benefit from
classification and load balancing to optimize performance and cost, while on
premise HPC systems benefit from using their native networking infrastructure.
Finally, we propose a novel approach for automatic detection of network
noise-based bottlenecks in cloud and on-premise HPC systems, which can be used
to improve resource allocation with existing resource managers or as part of a
new network and compute resource allocation framework.

redistributed regret that also achieves $\approx 5d$ bits per context for the
case of unknown context distribution and $0$ bits per context if the context
distribution is known.

propote a distributed learning algorithm that uses $\approx 2d$ bits per context
in the case of unknown context distribution and $0$ bits per context if the
context distribution is known, while achieving nearly the same regret bound as
if all contexts were directly observable. We also give a lower bound on the
redistributed regret that also achieves $\approx 2d$ bits per context for the
case of unknown context distribution and $0$ bits per context if the context
distribution is known.

the regret from below, and to bound the number of bits that need to be

psychological needs of autonomy, competence, and relatedness in the home
working environment. We conclude that the home working environment and the use
of Scrum both contribute to project success, with Scrum acting as a mediator.

communication, making time for team members to communicate with each other and
to conduct meetings, as well as providing tools that support the use of Scrum
