question-answer pairs that are difficult for models to answer with spurious
shortcuts. CONDAQA features 14,182 question-answer pairs with over 200 unique

performing model on CONDAQA (UnifiedQA-v2-3b) achieves only 42% on our
consistency metric, well below human performance which is 81%. We release our
dataset, along with fully-finetuned, few-shot, and zero-shot evaluations, to

opposites in the time evolution of a
quantum system: Annealing explores equilibrium phases of a Hamiltonian with
slowly changing parameters and can be exploited as a tool for solving complex
optimization problems. In contrast, quenches are sudden changes of the
Hamiltonian, producing a non-equilibrium situation. Here, we investigate the
relation between the two cases. Specifically, we show that the minimum of the
annealing gap, which is an important bottleneck of quantum annealing
algorithms, can be revealed from a dynamical quench parameter which describes
the dynamical quantum state after the quench. Combined with statistical tools
including the training of a neural network, the relation between quench and
annealing dynamics can be exploited to reproduce the full functional behavior
of the annealing gap from the quench data. We show that the partial or full
knowledge about the annealing gap which can be gained in this way can be used
to design optimized quantum annealing protocols with a practical
time-to-solution benefit. Our results are obtained from simulating random Ising
Hamiltonians, representing hard-to-solve instances of the exact cover problem.
We show that the functional behavior of the annealing gap across temperatures
has a direct connection to the mixing of the quantum state after the quench,
which allows to identify a minimum annealing time for each temperature,
indicating the minimum amount of quench time required to erase the initial
state. We find that the knowledge about the quench state provides the main
insights into the functional behavior of the annealing gap. These insights can
be exploited to design optimized quantum annealing protocols with a significant
time-to-solution benefit in terms of the total Hamiltonian evolution time as
well as the number of ancilla required in a practical quantum annealing
device.
  From a theoretical perspective, our work provides a connection between the
non-equilibrium physics of quench dynamics and the relevant system parameters
which is necessary for gaining knowledge on the equilibrium problem of the
annealing gap from the quench data. Besides that, our work shows how machine
learning tools can be used to extract this knowledge from the quench data. The
developed strategy to reproduce the annealing gap from the quench data can be
called "learning the annealing gap". From a practical point of view, the
knowledge gained about the annealing gap can be used to design optimized
quantum annealing protocols with a practical time-to-solution benefit.

  We demonstrate that a single backdoored sample with a dynamic trigger can
fool a pre-trained classifier at test time by activating the backdoor
functionality without any changes to its weights. We argue that this is due to
the memory of the classifier. We show that we can make use of adversarial
examples to increase this memory in both deterministic and stochastic
scenarios. Our experiments show that a classifier loaded into a device that
inferences on a dataset with a backdoor sample (whether poisoned during training
or not) is compromised, even if it was trained from scratch on a large
unpoisoned dataset. We argue that such global backdoor attacks are a greater
risk than local backdoor attacks, which typically occur due to specific
samples in the training dataset.

dynamic backdoor triggers. We force a classifier to a state such that the
backdoor is activated on all inputs; we show that such a state is unique and
acts like a fingerprint of the backdoor. We evaluate our detection mechanism
across different classes, trigger patterns, and percentages of poisoned
training data both in image classification and in tasks with more natural
inputs.
  In addition to backdoor attacks, we show that a global average pooling layer

compute a maximally sparse approximation to the reduced dynamics on it. The
recently released SSMLearn algorithm uses implicit optimization to fit a
spectral submanifold to data and reduce the dynamics to the normal form. Here,
we present two simplified algorithms, which reformulate manifold fitting and
normal form computation as explicit problems under certain assumptions. We show
on both numerical and experimental datasets that these algorithms yield
accurate and sparse rigorous models for essentially nonlinear (or

nonlinearities that can be captured by a spectral submanifold can be made
arbitrarily high by choosing a suitable parameterization of the SSM or by
incorporating auxiliary observed variables. This justifies the use of such

manifold instead of a submanifold, which is more suitable for systems with
asymmetric variables. We illustrate the benefits of data-driven model reduction
to obtain a roughly graded time scale separation in a prototypical experimental
setup. The algorithm is robust to noisy data and can be used to study periodic
oscillations as well as steady state dynamics.

dynamical system's structural properties, such as conservations laws, in the
reduced model. This is especially useful in chaotic systems where
nonlinearities are high, and where small imprecisions in the data (due to
noise or limited sampling) can lead to a loss of significant structure.

polypharmacy side effect identification, drug-drug interaction prediction and
combination therapy design tasks have been proposed. Here, we present a unified
theoretical view of relational machine learning models which can address these
tasks. We provide fundamental definitions, compare existing model architectures

  Relational machine learning models for drug data often handle very large
datasets with only sparse relational data. Recent proposals to address this
sparsity use pairwise interactions between single drug entities. We argue that
such models are insufficient as they are unable to capture polypharmacy
side-effects and are limited in their combination prediction generalizability
power. Hence, we argue that network-based approaches which simultaneously
model interactions between multiple drugs are more suitable for drug data.
Furthermore, we stress that models which try to learn from unstructured
side-effect descriptions can only be used as complementary approaches in
combination with network-based methods.
  The following tasks can be addressed using appropriate data and evaluation
procedures: (i) side-effect identification, (ii) drug-drug interaction
prediction, (iii) combination therapy design and (iv) drug replacement. For
each task, the most suitable data should be used, i.e. side-effect descriptions
for the first task and no descriptions for the others. We emphasize that
standardization of evaluation protocols across different datasets and
state-of-the-art method evaluations is crucial for further progress in this
domain.

highly relevant to human health. We emphasize that in order to build models
capable of handling real-world drug data, more detailed information on
drug-protein interactions is needed. With the increasing amount of available
information, relational machine learning models for drug data with outstanding
performance will likely be built. First steps towards evaluating the impact
of inductive biases have been made. More research in this direction is
necessary.

learning models for drug data to assist future related work. We hope to
encourage further research in this domain and possibly contribute towards

  Abstract:
  In this work we present two new approaches to solve the TOV
equations.
  Firstly, we consider a stellar object which contains two perfect fluids
with anisotropic pressure and obtain new exact solutions using a direct
resolution method. The unknown functions are thus directly determined from
the anisotrophic condition and the hydrostatic equilibrium of the star. This
approach is then applied to three different sets of anisotropic fluids for
which we obtain new exact solutions.
  Secondly, we consider a particular class of anisotropic two-fluid stars
and reconstruct the anisotropic pressure and energy density using a
reconstruction method. This technique allows to solve the anisotropic
hydrostatic equilibrium and energy conditions without directly solving the
anisotropic condition. We thus obtain another exact solution for the anisotropic
two-fluid star.
  Finally, we show that three of the generating theorems known for the single
fluid case can also be used to obtain two-fluid solutions from single fluid
ones. We thus demonstrate the connection between single and two-fluid
approaches.

galaxy evolution. In particular, major
mergers are able to have a transformative effect on galaxy morphology. In this
paper, we investigate the role of magnetic fields in gas-rich major mergers. To
this end, we run a series of high-resolution magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) zoom-in
simulations with the moving-mesh code Arepo and compare the outcome with
hydrodynamic simulations run from the same initial conditions. This is the
first time that the effect of magnetic fields in major mergers has been
investigated in a cosmologically-consistent manner. In contrast to previous
non-cosmological simulations, we find that the inclusion of magnetic fields has
a substantial impact on the production of the merger remnant. Whilst magnetic
fields do not strongly affect global properties, such as the star formation
history, they are able to significantly influence structural properties.
Indeed, MHD simulations consistently form remnants with extended discs and
well-developed spiral structure, whilst hydrodynamic simulations form more
compact remnants that display distinctive ring morphology. We support this work
with a resolution study and show that whilst global properties are broadly
converged across resolution and physics models, morphological differences only
develop given sufficient resolution. We argue that this is due to the more
efficient excitement of a small-scale dynamo in higher resolution simulations,
resulting in a more strongly amplified field that is better able to influence
gas distribution. Finally, we support our specific results with a study of gas
infiltration in mergers, showing that the formation of spiral structure is a
typical response to the interaction in gas-rich mergers, and that this is able
to be readily captured in cosmologically-consistent simulations.
  We highlight that the production of spiral structure in mergers is a
highly robust process, and is able to be captured in simulations with a
realistic treatment of physics, including magnetic fields. This process is able
to happen in real galaxies, and is likely an important mechanism for driving
star formation in line with the observations. Finally, we suggest that a
provisional lower limit for the scale of spiral structure that can form in
gas-rich major mergers is 10 kpc.
  Key words: magnetic fields; mergers; galaxy evolution; spiral arms

to search for dark
matter (DM). In lieu of the conventional approach of operating a tonne-scale
real-time detector to search for DM-induced nuclear recoils, paleo-detectors
take advantage of small samples of naturally occurring rocks on Earth that have
been deep underground ($\gtrsim 5$ km), accumulating nuclear damage tracks from
recoiling nuclei for $\mathcal{O}(1)$ Gyr. Modern microscopy techniques promise
the capability to read out nuclear damage tracks with nanometer resolution in
macroscopic samples. Thanks to their $\mathcal{O}(1)$ Gyr integration times,
paleo-detectors could constitute nuclear recoil detectors with keV recoil
energy thresholds and 100 kilotonne-yr exposures. This combination would allow
paleo-detectors to probe DM-nucleon cross sections orders of magnitude below
existing upper limits from conventional direct detection experiments. In this
article, we use improved background modeling and a new spectral analysis
technique to update the sensitivity forecast for paleo-detectors. We
demonstrate the robustness of the sensitivity forecast to the (lack of)
ancillary measurements of the age of the samples and the parameters controlling
the backgrounds, systematic mismodeling of the spectral shape of the
backgrounds, and the radiopurity of the mineral samples. Specifically, we
demonstrate that even if the uranium concentration in paleo-detectors is
double the expected value, the sensitivity of paleo-detectors would still be
able to probe $1\sigma$ smaller cross sections. We also discuss potential
contributions from spontaneous radioactive decays in the detector and from
extraterrestrial alpha particles, and show that they are subdominant to
radiation from primordial dust caught up in the Solar System.
  Based on the updated analysis, the previously estimated lower limit on the DM
cross section from paleo-detectors of $\sigma_{\mathrm{min}} \simeq 10^{-49}
\mathrm{erg~cm}^2$ should be increased to $\sigma_{\mathrm{min}} \simeq
10^{-46}\mathrm{erg~cm}^2$. We also update the predicted upper limit on the
Uranium concentration in paleo-detectors to $\lesssim 10^{-8}
\mathrm{kg~kg^{-1}}$.
  Paleo-detectors offer a novel approach to measuring the local density of DM
spinning within the Galactic halo

abundant and relatively easy to obtain, it is unclear how to leverage these
footage to learn meaningful ReID representations. In particular, most existing
unsupervised and domain adaptation ReID methods utilize only the public
datasets in their experiments, with labels removed. In addition, due to small
data sizes, these methods usually rely on fine tuning by the unlabeled training
data in the testing domain to achieve good performance. Inspired by the recent
progress of large-scale self-supervised image classification using contrastive
learning, we propose to learn ReID representation from large-scale unlabeled
surveillance video alone. Assisted by off-the-shelf pedestrian detection tools,
we apply the contrastive loss at both the image and the tracklet levels.
Together with a principal component analysis step using camera labels freely
available, our evaluation using a large-scale unlabeled dataset shows far
superior performance among unsupervised methods that do not use any training
data in the testing domain. Furthermore, the accuracy improves with the data
size and therefore our method has great potential with even larger and more
diversified datasets.

analyses: standing and moving. Our evaluation shows that it improves the
universe-wide verification accuracy by up to 25%. We also compare it with
existing unsupervised and domain adaptation ReID methods that use the following
frame Harris corner detection as the only underlying advanced camera state
estimation. Our method achieves much better performance under the same small
data setting.

the search ranking. It returns the correct target person among the top 3 queries

to ML training -- "Which training examples are 'guilty' in making the trained
ML model predictions inaccurate or unfair?" Modeling data influence for ML
training has attracted intensive interest over the last decade, and one popular
framework is to compute the Shapley value of each training example with respect
to utilities such as validation accuracy and fairness of the trained ML model.

only consider a single ML model "in isolation" and do not consider an
end-to-end ML pipeline that consists of data transformations, feature
extractors, and ML training.

computes Shapley values of training examples over an end-to-end ML pipeline,
and illustrate its applications in data debugging for ML training. To this end,
we first develop a novel algorithmic framework that computes Shapley value over
a specific family of ML pipelines that we call canonical pipelines: a positive
relational algebra query followed by a K-nearest-neighbor (KNN) classifier. We
show that, for many subfamilies of canonical pipelines, computing Shapley value
is in PTIME, contrasting the exponential complexity of computing Shapley value
in general. We then put this to practice -- given an sklearn dataset and a
relation specifying a subset of the dataset, the user can efficiently compute
the Shapley value of the data outside of the relation with respect to validation
accuracy of the ML pipeline that transforms, feature-extracts, and trains the
dataset. We further consider two applications of data debugging, removing
duplicate examples and bounding values, and show that it returns optimal
relations with respect to validation accuracy of the ML pipeline. We perform

we further design a hyperedge classifier in two well-working variants that
capture structural features in the projection. Extensive experiments validate

reconstruction, where the learned hypergraph can encode a dataset with a
lower-dimensional and more accurate hypergraph structure. Finally, as we
detailed, analyzing hyperedge distributions can offer new insights to graph and
hypergraph theories, and even physics and social science studies.

greater at lower temperatures, where the trapping frequency dominates the

of human beings. Scientific
literature, as the major medium that carries knowledge between scientists,
exhibits explosive growth during the last century. Despite the frequent use of
many tangible measures, such as citation, impact factor and g-index, to
quantify the influence of papers from different perspectives based on
scientific productivity, it has not yet been well understood how the
relationship between scientific productivity and knowledge amount turns out to
be, i.e., how the knowledge value of papers and knowledge amount vary with
development of the discipline. This raises the question of whether high
scientific productivity equals large knowledge amount. Here, building on rich
literature on academic conferences and journals, we collect 185 million
articles covering 19 disciplines published during 1970 to 2020, and establish
citation network research area to represent the knowledge flow from the authors
of the article being cited to the authors of the articles that cite it under
each specific area. As a result, the structure formed during the evolution of
each scientific area can implicitly tells how the knowledge flows between nodes
and how it behaves as the number of literature (productivity) increases. By
leveraging Structural entropy in structured high-dimensional space and Shannon
entropy in unstructured probability space, we propose the Quantitative Index of
Knowledge (KQI), which is taken as the subtraction between the two types of
entropy, to reflect the extent of disorder of the citation network. The higher
the KQI is, the more the knowledge flows, and the greater the knowledge amount
is. As a result, we can explicitly judge how the knowledge amount varies with
the growth of productivity from the perspective of the disorder of the citation
network. After thorough experimental design on 19 different academic areas, it
is found that the knowledge amount is generally increasing with the growth of
scientific productivity, and the greater the productivity, the more the
knowledge amount increases. In addition, our research indicates that the greater
the heterogeneity, the greater the knowledge amount generated by the same
productivity. Our study shows that the greater the productivity, the more the
disorder of the citation network, and the more the knowledge that can be
generated. In short, our approach unlocks the relationship between scientific
productivity and knowledge amount from the perspective of the disorder of the
citation network, and demonstrates how it specifically works through regional
structure analysis of the citation network.

approach to hypothesis testing, they are highly sensitive to details of the
data/model assumptions. Moreover it's not clear how straightforwardly this
approach can be implemented in practice, and in particular how sensitive it is
to the details of the computational implementation. Here, we investigate these
questions for Bayes factor analyses in the cognitive sciences. We explain the
statistics underlying Bayes factors as a tool for Bayesian inferences and
discuss that utility functions are needed for principled decisions on
hypotheses. Next, we study how Bayes factors misbehave under different
conditions. This includes a study of errors in the estimation of Bayes factors.
Importantly, it is unknown whether Bayes factor estimates based on bridge
sampling are unbiased for complex analyses. We are the first to use
simulation-based calibration as a tool to test the accuracy of Bayes factor
estimates. Moreover, we study how stable Bayes factors are against different
MCMC draws. We moreover study how Bayes factors depend on variation in the
data. We also look at variability of decisions based on Bayes factors and how
to optimize decisions using a utility function. We outline a Bayes factor
toolbox that can be used to simplify the process of conducting Bayes factor
analyses. We outline a pipeline that can be used to conduct Bayes factor
analyses in a principled way already in the design stage of a study. Finally,
we discuss open issues of Bayes factor analyses and how they can be addressed
with simulation studies.

easily implemented by users. We outline a checklist that should be followed
by researchers to conduct Bayes factor analyses.

statement and the appropriateness of the models. We recommend that researchers
spell out the defining features of the hypotheses and ensure that those are
captured by the models.

to different functional states in a wide range of applications, e.g., active
and resting states in the brain and stable and unstable power grid
configurations. For this reason, explosive synchronization transitions, which
facilitate fast, abrupt changes between these functional states, has recently
seen significant interest from researchers. While previous work has identified
properties of complex systems that support explosive synchronization, these
investigations have been conducted largely on an ad-hoc basis. Here we provide
an exact criterion for explosive synchronization in coupled phase oscillator
ensembles by investigating the necessary relationship between dynamical and
structural disorder. This result provides a critical step towards untangling
the intertwined properties of complex systems responsible for abrupt phase
transitions and bistability in biological and engineered systems.
Furthermore, we find that ensemble methods can facilitate interpretation of
high-dimensional data by reducing the data to a low-dimensional representation
of related systems. Using statistical analysis we find that a wide range of
structural and dynamical disorder schemes cross the exact boundary between
integrable and non-integrable systems at the same location on a map from
structural disorder to synchronization. However, transition shape and onset of
bistability vary widely between different ensemble schemes. Finally, we find
that the location of the synchronization transition relative to the
structural disorder of the system determines whether coupled oscillators will
exhibit bistability, which may be of importance to the control of biological
systems and the design of future biologicalinspired systems.
Thereby, we provide a framework that may be used to investigate and understand
the role of abrupt synchronization in biological and engineered systems.
What makes this framework important is that it may be applied to a wide range
of different system types, and may be used to answer questions about
ynchronization in biological and engineered systems, thereby informing future
research in these areas.

the detection of the GW spectrum produced by long-lasting sources such as
cosmic strings would provide a unique probe of particle physics parameters.

of the Standard Model. We illustrate this on a few examples, such as
supersymmetric models where the mass scale of scalar moduli and gravitino can

perfect synchronization between the swimmer's rotation and the elastic
relaxation of the tail. This, in turn, leads to a maximal persistence of the
tail's curl motion. A detailed analysis of the flow elicits that the increase
in swimming speed in the presence of viscoelasticity is mainly caused by an
increase of the recirculation of fluid around the swimmer body.

viscoelasticity on helical swimming motion, which could be used to design
swimmers that benefit the most from the non-Newtonian environment to achieve

transport and probe the interaction with other objects in the fluid (chemistry

numerous safety-critical computer vision applications, including human robot
interactions and automated driving. Real-world implementations will need to
guarantee their robustness against hardware soft errors corrupting the
underlying platform memory. Based on the previously observed efficacy of
activation clipping techniques, we build a prototypical safety case for
classifier CNNs by demonstrating that range supervision represents a highly
reliable fault detector and mitigator with respect to relevant bit flips,
adopting an eight-exponent floating point data representation. We further
explore novel, non-uniform range restriction methods that effectively suppress
the probability of silent data corruptions and uncorrectable errors. As a
safety-relevant end-to-end use case, we showcase the benefit of our approach in
a vehicle classification scenario, using ResNet-50 and the traffic camera data
set MIOVision. The quantitative evidence provided in this work can be leveraged
to inspire further and possibly more complex CNN safety arguments.
  We make our implementation of a safety-critical CNN benchmark, a vehicle
classifier trained on the MIOVision traffic camera dataset using ResNet-50, and
activation clipping techniques available at
https://github.com/fox1304/cnn_safety.
  We show that, with respect to bit flips, activation clipping (normalizing
activations to the range [-1, 1]) drastically reduces the failure rate by
approximately three orders of magnitude when compared to the baseline (no
countermeasures). Furthermore, we present that, with respect to data
corruptions and uncorrectable errors, it reduces the failure rate by about one
order of magnitude.
  By systematically evaluating the approach using a method based on fault
simulation and failure probability calculation, we show that activation
clipping is effective against bit flips, silent data corruptions, and
uncorrectable errors for CNN models trained with stochastic gradient descent.

potential building blocks of vision-based software, more reliable with respect
to hardware soft errors. This work can be used to inspire further and possibly
more complex CNN safety arguments.

new algorithms: the Sort-Backtrack (being faster than the Backtracking for

city, Santiago, suffered from widespread violence with public and private

non-local model that successfully described the French riots of 2005 to
incorporate the topology of Santiago's subway network and explain the reported
distribution of rioting activity in the city. Although the model reproduced the
disorders' aggregated temporal evolution, it could not deliver results
resembling the observed spatial distribution of activity on Santiago. The main
reason for this failure can be attributed to the fact that the model lacks a
population displacement mechanism, which seems vital to explain Santiago's
unrest episodes.
  From the model's failure, it is possible to point out two features that could
be incorporated to better simulate Chile's situation: the topology of the
city's subway network and a mechanism for population displacement.
  Furthermore, it is essential to stress that describing chaos with a scientific
approach is a delicate task, as the social context is intricate and deeply
shaped by political, economic, and cultural factors. The presentation of the
model should be accompanied by a discussion of its limitations and the need
for a multidisciplinary approach that considers the social science aspects of
the situation.
  Finally, it is essential to highlight that the purpose of studying extreme
events is to learn how to avoid them, and the present work has to be seen as a
step in this direction.

We revisit the question of what is our current knowledge of individual LMM
matrix elements without assuming unitarity. We define two minimal sets of
experimental constraints -- direct $+$ inherent bounds and indirect bounds, and
analyze the implications of each set on leptonic non-unitarity. In addition, we
clarify the treatment of flux and cross-section predictions, taking into
account NP contamination in hadronic inputs. We use the currently running
FASER$\nu$ experiment as a case study in order to demonstrate the sensitivity
of collider neutrino experiments to leptonic non-unitarity. We find that
indirect bounds constrain LMM non-unitarity to below the $10^{-3}$ level,
stronger than current CKM non-unitarity constraints. Conversely, considering
only direct and inherent bounds we find that ${\cal O}(1)$ unitarity violation
is viable at $2\sigma$, and will be probed by the FASER$\nu$ experiment in the
current run of the LHC.
  We stress that physicists often intuitively treat LMM constraints in a way
that resembles direct bounds on LMM elements, ignoring unitarity limits on
reconstruction. We demonstrate that such a treatment is incorrect and that it
leads to an underestimation of the unitarity violation that can be challenged by
experiment. In particular, charge current single neutrino processes have a
sensitivity to $(\mathcal{L}_\mu/E_\mu)^2$ and can be improved by requiring
same-flavor, opposite sign lepton pairs in the final state. We find that such a
requirement can reduce the uncertainty on individual LMM elements by up to
$40\%$.

parameters, and show that even in the presence of severe unitarity violation
$\sigma-2\sigma$ sensitivity to the standard three-flavor parameterization
cannot be claimed for the oscillation length, $\ell_{osc}$, with current or
future experimental bounds.
  We propose several methods to improve the analysis of individual LMM matrix
elements, and discuss their implementation in the context of neutrino production
processes.

takes into account the impact of unitarity

considered. Particularly, whether the algebra has generator by one vertex
operator or by several independent vertex operators depends on the highest
weight vector chosen. We study this algebra when the highest weight vector is
distinguished by a condition similar to the $C_2$-anomaly criterion for
logarithmic modules. Such a choice of highest weight vector is equivalent to
some specific conditions on the Dynkin diagram of $osp(1|2n)$. We find that
these conditions force a particular structure on the parafermion vertex operator
algebra associated to this module. Particularly, we prove that this algebra is
generated by one vertex operator in this case.

student model for a new task with the help of several decentralized teachers,
whose pre-training tasks and data are different and agnostic. Our motivation
for investigating such a problem setup stems from a recent dilemma of model
sharing. Many researchers or institutes have spent enormous resources on
training large and competent networks. Due to the privacy, security, or
intellectual property issues, they are, however, not able to share their own
pre-trained models, even if they wish to contribute to the community. The
proposed FedSA offers a solution to this dilemma and makes it one step further
since, again, the learned student may specialize in a new task different from
all of the teachers. To this end, we proposed a dedicated strategy for handling
FedSA. Specifically, our student-training process is driven by a novel
saliency-based approach that adaptively selects teachers as the participants
and integrates their representative capabilities into the student. To evaluate
the effectiveness of FedSA, we conduct experiments on both single-task and
multi-task settings. Experimental results demonstrate that FedSA effectively
amalgamates knowledge from decentralized models and achieves competitive
performance to centralized baselines.

evolution of Venus's atmosphere, leading to contemporary surface conditions,
remain hotly debated topics, and involve questions that tie into many
disciplines. We explore these various inter-related mechanisms which shaped the
evolution of the atmosphere, starting with the volatile sources and sinks.
Going from the deep interior to the top of the atmosphere, we describe volcanic
outgassing, surface atmosphere interactions, and atmosphere escape.
Furthermore, we address more complex aspects of the history of Venus, including
the role of Late Accretion impacts, how magnetic field generation is tied into
long-term evolution, and the implications of geochemical and geodynamical
feedback cycles for atmospheric evolution. We highlight plausible end-member
evolutionary pathways that Venus could have followed, from accretion to its
present-day state, based on modeling and observations. In a first scenario, the
planet was desiccated by atmospheric escape during the magma ocean phase. In a
second scenario, Venus could have harbored surface liquid water for long
periods of time, until its temperate climate was destabilized and it entered a
runaway greenhouse phase. In a third scenario, Venus's inefficient outgassing
could have kept water inside the planet, where hydrogen was trapped in the core
and the mantle was oxidized. We discuss the requirements for each scenario and
how they are constrained by observations. We highlight the differences between
planets with magnetic fields and those without, suggesting that magnetic
field generation could be tied into long-term evolution. Finally, we propose an
alternative view of the magnetic field formation in Venus-like planets, where
the initial field could be generated by a Late Accretion impact carrying a
large dust grain, rather than the traditional dynamo process.

model event-type data such
as natural disasters, online message exchanges, financial transactions or
neuronal spike trains. One very popular point process model in which the
probability of occurrences of new events depend on the past of the process is
the Hawkes process. In this work we consider the nonlinear Hawkes process,
which notably models excitation and inhibition phenomena between dimensions of
the process. In a nonparametric Bayesian estimation framework, we obtain
concentration rates of the posterior distribution on the parameters, under mild
assumptions on the prior distribution and the model. These results also lead to
convergence rates of Bayesian estimators. Another object of interest in
event-data modelling is to recover the graph of interaction - or Granger
connectivity graph - of the phenomenon. We provide consistency guarantees on
Bayesian methods for estimating this quantity; in particular, we prove that the
posterior distribution is consistent on the graph adjacency matrix of the
process, as well as a Bayesian estimator based on an adequate loss function.
Finally, we obtain a convergence rate on the posterior mean error, as well as a
concentration rate of the MCMC algorithm in a pseudo-marginal framework. The
notion of "close" processes is formalized through a metric which measures the
difference between the "past history" of two processes. The main novelty with
respect to existing works is to obtain concentration rates on the posterior
distribution, as well as convergence rates on Bayesian estimators and MCMC
algorithms, under conditions which are not too strong on the prior distribution
and the model.

micro-earthquake data in Michigan, and temporal data of notifications of the
Spread of Infectious Disease in Iceland. In both scenarios we illustrate the
advantages of nonlinear Hawkes processes, namely the capacity to model a
reasonable number of dimensions. We also illustrate the benefits of using MCMC
within our specific setting, by considering other models which are able to take
only a small number of interactions into account. Finally, we show that the
Bayesian estimator for the adjacency matrix of the process is able to recover
nontrivial patterns in the data, even in the general setting of not being able
to know the "true" parameters.

H) is positioned as having ideal
conservation properties. When properly implemented, conservation of total mass,
energy, and both linear and angular momentum is guaranteed exactly, up to
machine precision. This is particularly important for some applications in
computational astrophysics, such as binary dynamics, mergers, and accretion of
compact objects (neutron stars, black holes, and white dwarfs). However, in
astrophysical applications that require the inclusion of gravity, calculating
pairwise particle interactions becomes prohibitively expensive. In the Fast
Multipole Method (FMM), they are, therefore, replaced with symmetric
interactions between distant clusters of particles (contained in the tree
nodes) Although such an algorithm is linear momentum-conserving, it introduces
spurious torques that violate conservation of angular momentum. We present a
modification of FMM that is free of spurious torques and conserves angular
momentum explicitly. The new method has practically no computational overhead
compared to the standard FMM.
  We test the new method with a set of rigorous tests, where exact solution
exists, and demonstrate its accuracy and stability in both particle and
grid-based implementations. We also perform a set of astrophysical simulations,
including binary mergers, accretion of compact objects, and large N particle
dynamics, to demonstrate that it is suitable for real astrophysical
applications.
  In the description of the algorithm, we focus on the SPH formulation, which
is the most complex, while mentioning corresponding modifications for Grid
methods. Our code is based on GPHF (General Particle Hydrodynamics with Fast
Gravity Compilation), and for convenience, we make it available for readers to
ease implementation into their codes.
  Conserved angular momentum is an important probe of rotational dynamics in
astrophysical simulations. It can help to diagnose incorrect gravity or
integration schemes. We propose a simple test for conservation of angular
momentum in hydrodynamic simulations that can be used to tune up algorithms.
When applied to a set of test scenarios, it helps to optimize the mass
compaction criterion in our implementation.
  We show that the new method is computationally free of overhead compared to
the standard FMM. While it is currently the fastest way to compute gravity for
our large N simulations, the new method is preferable in cases when precise
conservation of angular momentum is required, such as in binary dynamics or
when many compact objects are present in the same simulation.

assist training has a potential for improving the model's performance. However,
it is further challenged by the cross-anatomy domain shift due to the different
appearance and even imaging modalities from the target structure. To solve this
problem, we propose Contrastive Semi-supervised learning for Cross Anatomy
Domain Adaptation (CS-CADA) that adapts a model to segment similar structures
in a target domain, which requires only limited annotations in the target
domain by leveraging a set of existing annotated images of similar structures

consistency constraint. Extensive experiments show that our CS-CADA is able to
solve the challenging cross-anatomy domain shift problem, achieving accurate

annotations, it also achieves better performance compared to the multi-domain

(sometimes called a `trick') is the cornerstone of
modern supergravity. In this paper, the free massive Wess--Zumino theory is
used as a simple toy model to look at the BRS symmetry of the first, second and
1.5 order formalisms. This easily shows that the 1.5 order formalism is flawed
for all theories. The 1.5 algebra naively appears to close. However, when it is
analyzed in detail, in a simple model, where easy calculations are available,
the 1.5 formalism always generates an invalid BRS operator, which is not even
nilpotent. This clearly is also the case for supergravity. It follows that a
revised and completed set of nilpotent first order supergravity transformations
is needed to properly understand 3+1 dimensional supergravity. Such a set seems
easy to write down, by simply adding two more auxiliary fields so that the spin
connection becomes part of a super--YM multiplet.
  Finally, it is interesting to ask if the 1.5 order formalism could ever work
for other theories. Clearly, for all theories built with BRS invariant
actions, the answer is no. However, for theories that do not have a BRS
invariance, like some versions of non--linear electrodynamics, the 1.5 formalism
could, maybe, work. However, as it also breaks BRS at the quantum level, in
terms of a non nilpotent BRS operator, it is not worthwhile to explore this
further.
  The paper is concluded with some remarks about the status of supergravity and
its possible completion.
  Appendices contain all the technical details of the BRS symmetry analysis of
the 1.5 order formalism for the complex scalar and Dirac fermion fields and of
supergravity.

high-power laser pulses becomes a growing challenge for conventional
solid-state optics due to their limited damage threshold. As a result,
plasma-based optical components which can sustain extremely high fields are
attracting increasing interest. Here, we propose a type of plasma waveplate
based on magneto-optical birefringence under a transverse magnetic field, which
can work under extremely high laser power. Importantly, this waveplate can
simultaneously alter the polarization state and boost the peak laser power. It
is demonstrated numerically that an initially linearly polarized laser pulse
with 5 petawatt peak power can be converted into a circularly polarized pulse
with a peak power higher than 10 petawatts by such a waveplate with a
centimeter-scale diameter. The energy conversion efficiency of the polarization
transformation is about $98\%$. The necessary waveplate thickness is shown to
scale inversely with plasma electron density $n_e$ and the square of magnetic
field $B_0$, and it is about 1 cm for $n_e=3\times 10^{20}$ cm$^{-3}$ and
$B_0=100$ T. The proposed plasma waveplate and other plasma-based optical
components can play a critical role for the effective utilization of
multi-petawatt laser systems.
  We also propose a scheme to realize a plasma-based laser amplifier by which
the gain medium can be driven to a strongly nonlinear state with
self-sustaining magnetic field, and the fields of the pump and amplified beams
can be controlled by magnetic fields, respectively. With this amplifier, the
peak power of a chirped initial laser pulse can be converted into a nearly
transform limited pulse. The gain material can be optically thick so that the
average power can be increased by thousands of times. Combined with a
waveplate, the amplifier can also be used to generate high-power ultrashort
pulses.
  Both of these proposals illustrate the huge advantage of using plasma
media for laser power enhancement and control. They also indicate a new
direction for the development of laser-powered optical components and tools

Pontrjagin classes of a differential manifold. We give an expanded version of

Gaussian random field manifolds using the first and second fundamental forms
(Fisher information matrices). Using Markov Chain Monte Carlo techniques, we
simulate the dynamics of these random fields and compute the Gaussian curvature
of the parametric space, analyzing how this quantity changes along phase
transitions. During the simulation, we have observed an unexpected phenomenon
that we called the \emph{curvature effect}, which indicates that a highly
asymmetric geometric deformation happens in the underlying parametric space
when there are significant increase/decrease in the system's entropy. This
asymmetric pattern relates to the emergence of hysteresis, leading to an
intrinsic arrow of time along the dynamics.
  We show that the curvature effect is a necessary condition for the
hysteresis emergence in these random fields. This paper contributes to the
establishment of a link between medium geometric effects and hysteresis
emergence, leading to a new perspective on the understanding of this crucial
feature of complex systems.

the underlying parametric space, revealing that the assumption of a flat space
is not valid for these random fields.

to investigate if the hysteresis emergence is a common feature among random
fields or if it is a feature restricted to specific models.

$\ell_1$-norm principal component analysis (L1-PCA) as a typical robust
alternative of the conventional PCA has enjoyed great popularity over the past
years. In this work, we consider a rotationally invariant L1-PCA, which is
hardly studied in the literature. To tackle it, we propose a proximal
alternating linearized minimization method with a nonlinear extrapolation for
solving its two-block reformulation. Moreover, we show that the proposed method
converges at least linearly to a limiting critical point of the reformulated
problem. Such a point is proved to be a critical point of the original problem
under a condition imposed on the step size. Finally, we conduct numerical
experiments on both synthetic and real datasets to support our theoretical
developments and demonstrate the efficacy of our approach.
  As L1-PCA is an optimization problem, to which many existing solutions are
available, one may question the necessity of proposing a new solver for it.
To address this, we explain that the rotationally invariant L1-PCA is in fact
a nonconvex subspaces separation problem, for which the extrapolation step in
our solver is necessary. This is demonstrated through the failure of all the
existing L1-PCA solvers when applied to the rotationally invariant setting. It
is interesting to note that this extrapolation is done in a way that is
different from the existing density-free extrapolation techniques. Moreover,
we show that the extrapolation helps to improve the convergence of the
reformulation even for the conventional L1-PCA.

necessary for solving the rotationally invariant L1-PCA. While it is difficult
to claim that a new solver is necessary for L1-PCA when considered in its
conventional setting, our theoretical and experimental results demonstrate
that such a solver is indeed useful for solving the reformulated problem and
all the existing L1-PCA solvers for the conventional setting perform poorly
when applied to the rotationally invariant setting.

planning module to evaluate the feasibility and efficiency of our map
representation. The system is validated in a simulation environment and a
demonstration in the real world is conducted. In addition, the HiTMap is made
available open-source.

obstacle avoidance, and path planning. Our code provides a feasible
implementation of a navigation system from detection to planning. The code is

isolated system, where the concept of dissipated work is not clear. The trick
is shown to be thermodynamically consistent and can be extremely useful in
simulation. We justify that it is the thermodynamic average of the internal
microwork done by a microstate that is dissipated; this microwork is different

studies on pre-trained representation learning models, which show that rich
linguistic features such as parts-of-speech and morphology are encoded by them.

oversensitive. To get around the issue of dataset bias, we enforce the
feature extraction capability of rich contextual embedding models such as BERT
into the scoring model, following a multi-task learning paradigm. The
experimental results show that one can make AES models less oversensitive and
less brittle by incorporating contextual understanding and language structure
features.

cancer diagnosis, but it is
labor-intensive, in which tasks such as cell detection, classification, and
counting are particularly prominent. A common solution for automating these
tasks is using nucleus segmentation technology. However, it is hard to train a
robust nucleus segmentation model, due to several challenging problems, the
nucleus adhesion, stacking, and excessive fusion with the background. Recently,
some researchers proposed a series of automatic nucleus segmentation methods
based on point annotation, which can significant improve the model performance.
Nevertheless, the point annotation needs to be marked by experienced
pathologists. In order to take advantage of segmentation methods based on point
annotation, further alleviate the manual workload, and make cancer diagnosis
more efficient and accurate, it is necessary to develop an automatic nucleus
detection algorithm, which can automatically and efficiently locate the
position of the nucleus in the pathological image and extract valuable
information for pathologists. In this paper, we propose a W-shaped network for
automatic nucleus detection. Different from the traditional U-Net based method,
mapping the original pathology image to the target mask directly, our proposed
method split the detection task into two sub-tasks. The first sub-task maps the
original pathology image to the binary mask, then the binary mask is mapped to
the density mask in the second sub-task. After the task is split, the task's
difficulty is significantly reduced, and the density mask can be efficiently
obtained by simple binary operation, and the final target mask can be obtained
by reverse operation. By comparing the experimental results of our method with
the U-Net method, it is obvious that our method can improve the detection
performance by 5.88%. Meanwhile, our proposed method can reduce the average
post-processing time by 35.79% per image.

state variables and rewards and identify conditions under which an MDP with
exogenous state can be decomposed into an exogenous Markov Reward Process
involving only the exogenous state+reward and an endogenous Markov Decision

variance-covariance condition under which Monte Carlo policy evaluation on the
endogenous MDP is accelerated compared to using the full MDP. Similar speedups
are likely to carry over to all RL algorithms. We develop two algorithms for
discovering the exogenous variables and test them on several MDPs. Results show
that the algorithms are practical and can significantly speed up reinforcement

are exogenous. We define semi-exogenous state variables and develop a
corresponding decomposition of the MDP into two processes: a low-dimensional
exogenous process and a high-dimensional endogenous process. We also derive a
variance lower bound for Monte Carlo policy evaluation on the endogenous
process and show that by ignoring the exogenous variables, the variance can
increase by an exponential factor. We test the notion on several MDPs and find
that the gain due to decomposition is significant.
  Both works point to a simple yet powerful idea: if you have extra state that
is changing in a way that is not related to your actions, then ignore it. This
is true in the semi-exogenous setting, where we have established conditions for
state that are clearly useful, and it is likely true in other settings as well.
For example, in stochastic physics environments, it is likely useful to ignore
the initial random fluctuations that are uncontrolled by the actions. We have
not attempted to formalize such a notion, but it is a promising direction for

  This observation leads to a generalization to pseudocodes which we call {\it
logical pseudocodes}. It is similar to natural deduction proof of computability
logic\cite{Jap03,Jap08}. Each statement in it corresponds to a proof step in
natural deduction. Therefore, the merit over pseudocode is that each statement
is guaranteed to be correct and safe with respect to the initial
specifications. It can also be seen as an extension to computability logic web
(\colw) with forward reasoning capability.
  We introduce a semantics on it by interpreting each proof node (or each statement
in pseudocode) as its least fixed point. We show that it corresponds to
\colw's semantics. An algorithm (a logical pseudocode) is realized as a
computation (a proof tree) which achieves the initial specifications through
forward reasoning. They are equivalent in terms of correctness and safety.
  We also introduce a characterization of it by elementary logic. We reveal
that it is equivalent to elementary logic with the following two rules in addition to those of \colw\ : cut and while.
  The logical pseudocode is a generalization of tail recursion. It allows for
directed search towards the goal. It is also an optimization of backtracking.

scheduling problem. It also achieves polynomial time complexity in the
optimization of database query and Murray's example.

three typical problems of backtracking, achieves better performance in several
applications, and has the advantage of directed search towards the goal.

CT denoising thanks to its superior performance despite the fast computational
time. In particular, cycleGAN has been demonstrated as a powerful unsupervised
learning scheme to improve the low-dose CT image quality without requiring
matched high-dose reference data. Unfortunately, one of the main limitations of
the cycleGAN approach is that it requires two deep neural network generators at
the training phase, although only one of them is used at the inference phase.
The secondary auxiliary generator is needed to enforce the cycle-consistency,
but the additional memory requirement and increases of the learnable parameters
are the main huddles for cycleGAN training. To address this issue, here we
propose a novel cycleGAN architecture using a single switchable generator. In
particular, a single generator is implemented using adaptive instance
normalization (AdaIN) layers so that the baseline generator converting a
low-dose CT image to a routine-dose CT image can be switched to a generator
converting high-dose to low-dose by simply changing the AdaIN code. Thanks to
the shared baseline network, the additional memory requirement and weight
increases are minimized, and the training can be done more stably even with
small training data. Experimental results show that the proposed method
outperforms the previous cycleGAN approaches while using only about half the
parameters.

continuum, we investigate the rotational motion of deformed halos in $^{42}$Mg

particle bound states and the continuum not only in the ground state but also
in rotational states after angular momentum projection. For $^{42}$Mg, we
identify a deformed halo state with a small excitation energy of 0.78 MeV in

its ability to autonomously extract kinetic features, which is crucial for
super-resolving distorted frames that only provide static information. To this
end, we use a feature extraction metric that measures the amplitude of
motion-related features. BasicVSR++ extracts kinetic features better than its
constituent components, which explains its superior performance on difficult
video frames. As a result, BasicVSR++ can better exploit the kinetic features
across misaligned frames and thus achieves improved reconstruction performance

acceptable in real applications. In particular, we show that BasicVSR++ is
robust to over-fitting to raw data, thanks to the minimal parameters. It can

  We propose a novel approach to communicate a desired structure over a
quantum channel, which requires less quantum bits (qubits) than an equivalent
classical communication of the same information. In this communication, we
utilize negativity of a shared quantum state among observers, as a quantitative
measure of quantumness. This is facilitated by exploiting an inequality involving
partial trace and norm, which is an extension of the quantum discord inequality.
This new approach yields a non-classical enhancement of existing quantum
communication protocols such as superdense coding and quantum key distribution.
In particular, we show that their fidelity and security are enhanced by
information about quantumness of the shared state. We also show how to enhance
the amount of classical information that can be transmitted classicalely over
a quantum channel by using the information about quantumness of the shared
state. We observe that the amount of classical information that can be transmitted
classically over a quantum channel increases with the amount of quantumness of
the shared state. This is similar to classical capacity of a quantum channel,
which is also increased with the amount of quantumness of the shared state.
Moreover, we show how to switch the quantumness of a shared state from one
group of observers to another group of observers, which is useful for quantum
cooperation. In particular, we show how to increase the amount of quantumness
of the shared state among a group of observers by using less quantumness of
the original shared state among all the observers. We illustrate our findings
with a series of spin shared states among observers.

PSR B1133+16, from which we have obtained high-quality dynamic spectra and
their associated scintillation arcs, arising from the scattering screens
located along the line of sight to the pulsar. We have identified six
individual scattering screens that are responsible for the observed

scattering screens have not changed significantly in this time, we have modeled

information about the placement, orientation, and velocity of five of the six

these screens with an under-dense region of the Local Bubble.

convolution neural networks (PDCNNs). Specifically, as a probabilistic

long- and short-term dependencies of quasi-periodic signals such as speech. The
performances of single-tone sinusoid and speech generations are evaluated. The

a suitable incoming plane wavelet with compact support in the propagation

incoming plane wavelet; \emph{iii)} reconstruction of the time-harmonic
solution from the time-domain solution via a Fourier transform in time. An
essential ingredient of the new method is a front-tracking mesh adaptation

support of the wave front, this allows us to make the number of the required
degrees of freedom to reach a given accuracy significantly less dependent on

Fourier transform in \emph{iii)} that exploits the reduced number of degrees of

of translating speech in one language
into text in another language. Traditional cascaded approaches for ST, using
Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) and Machine Translation (MT) systems, are
prone to error propagation. End-to-end approaches use only one system to avoid
propagating error, yet are difficult to employ due to data scarcity. We explore
zero-shot translation, which enables translating a pair of languages that is
unseen during training, thus avoid the use of end-to-end ST data. Zero-shot
translation has been shown to work for multilingual machine translation, yet
has not been studied for speech translation. We attempt to build zero-shot ST
models that are trained only on ASR and MT tasks but can do ST task during
inference. The challenge is that the representation of text and audio is
significantly different, thus the models learn ASR and MT tasks in different
ways, making it non-trivial to perform zero-shot. These models tend to output
the wrong language when performing zero-shot ST. We tackle the issues by
including additional training data and an auxiliary loss function that
minimizes the text-audio difference. Our experiment results and analysis show
that the methods are promising for zero-shot ST. Moreover, our methods are
particularly useful in the few-shot settings where a limited amount of ST data
is available, with improvements of up to +11.8 BLEU scores.

potentials over general
2-D domains is a subject of great importance for the numerical solution of
Poisson's equation and volume integral equations. Complicated domains typically
require discretization by unstructured meshes, over which the direct evaluation
of the potential by quadrature becomes costly. In this paper, we present a
simple and efficient high-order algorithm for computing Newtonian potentials,
based on the use of Green's third identity for transforming the volume integral
into a collection of boundary integrals, which can be easily handled by the
Helsing-Ojala method. As a result, the time cost of the classically expensive
near field and self-interaction computations over an unstructured mesh becomes
roughly the same as the time cost of the FMM-based far field interaction
computation. One of the key components of our algorithm is the high-order 2-D
monomial approximation of a function over a mesh element, which is often
regarded as an ill-conditioned problem, since it involves the solution of a
Vandermonde linear system. In fact, it has long been observed that, when the
function is sufficiently smooth, and when a backward stable linear system
solver is used, the resulting monomial expansion can approximate the function
uniformly to high accuracy. We rigorously formalize this observation in this
paper. The performance of our algorithm is illustrated through several
numerical experiments.
  We also consider the special case of computing self-interactions for piecewise
linear functions in 2D. For a degree $k$ monomial, the cost of evaluating the
boundary integrals using a high-order method is $O(k^3)$, which is quite high
for large $k$. If we know that the function has sufficient smoothness, e.g.
it is a $C^2$ function, we can reduce this cost to $O(k^2)$ by approximating
the function with a sum of monomials. The new monomial expansion can be used
to compute the self-interaction. We also illustrate this approach with some
numerical examples.
  Finally, we consider the classical problem of recovering a height function
from its downward facing obstacle in a plane. We consider two methods for this
problem: one based on the use of volume derivatives and another based on the
use of boundary derivatives. We analyze these methods in the limit of large
scale factors and also experiment with them numerically.
